pattern.note: Practice set, not a mock; original passages and questions (none taken from Mock 01-06). The official paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes; this set is longer for extra practice.

subjects_covered: Law of Contract and Government Contracts
instructions: Each question has four options and exactly one correct answer.
Correct answer carries 1 mark; each wrong answer carries -0.25.
Passages are original summaries for practice. Verify pending/evolving matters (e.g. reference proceedings) against current official sources.
Every explanation includes why the other options fail, the CLAT trap, and any language trick.

passages.title: Citizenship, Assam Accord and Section 6A
passages.passage: The Assam Accord of 15 August 1985 ended the Assam agitation against illegal migration. To implement it, Parliament enacted the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985, inserting Section 6A in the Citizenship Act, 1955. Persons of Indian origin who came to Assam from the specified territory before 1 January 1966 and have since been ordinarily resident are deemed citizens from 1 January 1966. Those who came on or after 1 January 1966 but before 25 March 1971, and were detected as foreigners, must register; they become citizens ten years after the date of detection and have no right to vote in the meantime. Persons entering on or after 25 March 1971 are outside the section and remain illegal migrants. On 17 October 2024, a Constitution Bench upheld Section 6A by a majority of 4:1. The majority held that Articles 6 and 7 deal with persons migrating at or around the commencement of the Constitution and do not exhaust Parliament's power, which flows from Article 11 notwithstanding Articles 5 to 10. It held that Article 14 was not offended by confining the scheme to Assam, since Assam had borne a proportionately far heavier burden of migration relative to its area and population, and that 25 March 1971, the date on which the Bangladesh Liberation War began, was a rational cut-off. The Article 29(1) challenge failed: the right of any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture to conserve it is not a right to exclude others, and the petitioners had to show that the presence of migrants actually impaired that conservation. The argument that migration amounted to 'external aggression' under Article 355 was rejected. Justice Pardiwala dissented, holding that Section 6A, though valid when enacted, had become unconstitutional with the passage of time, because its open-ended operation produced temporal unreasonableness and manifest arbitrariness.

questions.question: Ramiz, of Indian origin, entered Assam from the specified territory on 10 March 1968 and has lived there continuously. He was detected as a foreigner on 15 June 1990 and registered. On Section 6A as described, he

options.A: becomes a citizen on 15 June 2000, ten years after detection, and cannot vote until then
options.B: remains an illegal migrant, since entry after 1 January 1966 takes a person outside the section
options.C: is deemed a citizen from 1 January 1966, since he entered before the 25 March 1971 cut-off
options.D: becomes a citizen on 10 March 1978, ten years after entry, and may vote throughout

questions.explanation: Entry between 1 January 1966 and 25 March 1971 places him in the middle class: he registers, becomes a citizen ten years after detection and is disenfranchised meanwhile.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B confuses the two cut-offs: deemed citizenship is only for pre-1966 entrants. Option C runs the ten-year clock from entry rather than detection. Option D treats 1966 as the line of illegality when it is 25 March 1971.
questions.clat_trap: Two dates and a detection date are planted so that candidates run the clock from the wrong event or misread which cut-off creates illegality.
questions.language_trick: The clock runs 'from the date of detection', not from entry; 'before the cut-off' in one option tempts a 'pre-1971 means deemed citizen' shortcut.

questions.question: In upholding the confinement of the scheme to Assam, the majority reasoned that

options.A: Assam is the only State that shares a border with Bangladesh, so the classification followed from geography alone
options.B: Article 14 has no application to legislation on citizenship made under Article 11
options.C: the Assam Accord was a political settlement and therefore outside judicial review under Article 14
options.D: Assam had borne a proportionately heavier burden of migration, giving the classification a rational basis

questions.explanation: The majority applied the ordinary classification test: an intelligible differentia (disproportionate burden) with a rational nexus to the object.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B are invented shortcuts that avoid Article 14 review, which the Court did not do. Option C is factually wrong: other States also border Bangladesh.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option sounds like a plausible judicial shortcut. Only the correct option shows the classification test actually being applied.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which proposition on Article 29(1) is consistent with the majority holding?

options.A: A section of citizens may conserve its culture, but that is not a right to exclude others, and impairment of the culture must actually be shown
options.B: Article 29(1) is violated whenever demographic change occurs, since culture is conserved only through exclusive occupation
options.C: Article 29(1) cannot be invoked against a statute and is enforceable only against executive action
options.D: Article 29(1) is available only to religious and linguistic minorities, not to a numerically dominant community

questions.explanation: The Court read the right as one to conserve, not to exclude, and required proof of actual impairment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B contradicts the text, which says 'any section of citizens', not 'minorities'. Option C equates conservation with exclusion, the very argument rejected. Option D has no basis in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates often import the minority-only reading of Article 29. The Article speaks of 'any section of citizens'.
questions.language_trick: 'any section of citizens' versus 'minorities' is the textual trap.

questions.question: Justice Pardiwala's dissent differs from the majority in holding that Section 6A

options.A: is valid in principle, but the cut-off date should be moved forward by the Court to a date it considers just
options.B: was void from its inception for want of legislative competence, since Article 11 does not authorise any later citizenship law of this kind
options.C: was valid when enacted but became unconstitutional with time, because its open-ended operation made it unreasonable and arbitrary
options.D: violates Article 29(1) because it extinguishes the distinct culture of Assam and the language and script of its indigenous people

questions.explanation: The dissent found supervening invalidity, not invalidity at birth.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A would be a void ab initio finding, which is not what the dissent held. Option B is a ground the majority rejected, not the dissent's reasoning. Option D is a remedy the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The distinction between invalid from the start and invalid by later operation is the whole point, and is easily missed in the hurry of reading options.
questions.language_trick: 'though valid when enacted' signals supervening unconstitutionality, as opposed to void ab initio.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the majority opinion?

options.A: The choice of 25 March 1971 as the cut-off was rational, being linked to the events surrounding Bangladesh
options.B: Large-scale migration into Assam by itself amounts to 'external aggression', obliging expulsion
options.C: Parliament's power over citizenship under Article 11 operates notwithstanding Articles 5 to 10 of the Constitution
options.D: Articles 6 and 7 do not exhaust Parliament's power to make provision for later migrants into the territory

questions.explanation: The majority rejected the 'external aggression' argument.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D each restate a holding of the majority.
questions.clat_trap: Negative framing: three options are true restatements and the single false one is a dramatic-sounding proposition.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT consistent' reverses the usual hunt for the true statement.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Parliament could enact Section 6A even though Articles 6 and 7 already deal with persons who migrated around the commencement of the Constitution. Reason (R): Articles 6 and 7 exhaust Parliament's power over citizenship, so that only a constitutional amendment could have authorised Section 6A.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is correct because Article 11 gives Parliament plenary power. R is the opposite of the majority's reasoning.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R reverses the holding that Articles 6 and 7 do not exhaust Parliament's power.
questions.clat_trap: R is a mirror image of the actual reasoning and is attractive to candidates who recall 'Articles 6 and 7' without the holding.
questions.language_trick: 'exhaust' and 'only' make R absolute.

passages.title: Article 370: Temporary Provision, Article 367 and President's Rule
passages.passage: Article 370 appears in Part XXI, headed 'Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions'. It limited Parliament's power over Jammu and Kashmir and, under clause (3), allowed the President to declare the Article inoperative on the recommendation of the State's Constituent Assembly, which dissolved in 1957 without making any recommendation. In August 2019, while the State was under President's Rule, the President issued C.O. 272, which, using Article 367, read 'Constituent Assembly' in Article 370(3) as 'Legislative Assembly', and then C.O. 273 declaring Article 370 inoperative. Parliament enacted the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, creating the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir (with a legislature) and Ladakh (without one). On 11 December 2023, in In re Article 370 of the Constitution, a five-judge Bench, in concurring opinions, upheld the abrogation. It held that Article 370 was a temporary provision, that Jammu and Kashmir retained no internal sovereignty after accession, and that the President's power under clause (3) survived the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly, since a contrary view would make a temporary provision permanent. The Court held that using Article 367 to substitute 'Legislative Assembly' for 'Constituent Assembly' was impermissible, being an amendment of Article 370 by interpretation, but sustained C.O. 273 because the President could in any event exercise the clause (3) power. On the exercise of State powers by Parliament under President's Rule, it held that such actions are not invalid merely because they are irreversible, and are open to challenge only if mala fide or without reasonable nexus to the purpose of the Proclamation. The creation of Ladakh as a Union Territory was upheld under Article 3. Whether a State may be converted into a Union Territory was left open in view of the Union's assurance that statehood would be restored, and the Election Commission was directed to hold Assembly elections by 30 September 2024.

questions.question: The heading of Part XXI figured in the 2023 decision principally to support the conclusion that

options.A: Jammu and Kashmir retained residual internal sovereignty during the transitional period
options.B: the Article could be repealed only by the amending procedure of Article 368 and not by Presidential order
options.C: the power to end the Article lapsed once the Constituent Assembly dissolved, since temporary provisions expire with the body they mention
options.D: Article 370 was a transitional arrangement and could not be read as conferring permanent special status

questions.explanation: Text and placement showed a temporary arrangement, and a contrary reading would make a temporary provision permanent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the inversion of the Court's reasoning. Option B was rejected expressly. Option C was not the holding.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options borrow the vocabulary of 'temporary' and 'transitional' to build conclusions the Court rejected.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The 2019 Presidential orders survived although the Article 367 route was held impermissible, because

options.A: Article 367 validly allowed 'Legislative Assembly' to replace 'Constituent Assembly' as a matter of ordinary interpretation of the text
options.B: the President could independently exercise the clause (3) power, so the defective route did not vitiate the result
options.C: the Union's assurance of restoring statehood validated the orders retrospectively
options.D: the later enactment of the Reorganisation Act cured any defect in the process of the Presidential orders

questions.explanation: The clause (3) power survived dissolution, so C.O. 273 stood on its own footing.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the holding that the Article 367 route was an amendment in disguise. Option C and Option D state cures the Court did not rely on.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates who remember only 'abrogation upheld' wrongly assume the Article 367 route was also upheld.
questions.language_trick: 'although ... impermissible' flags a split outcome: the route failed, the result stood.

questions.question: On acts of Parliament under a Proclamation of President's Rule in the State, the Court held that such acts

options.A: non-justiciable, because the satisfaction behind a Proclamation cannot be examined by a court even on grounds of mala fides
options.B: not invalid merely for irreversibility, but open to challenge if mala fide or lacking a nexus with the purpose
options.C: dependent on confirmation by a newly elected State Legislature to remain valid once the Proclamation has been revoked
options.D: confined to the powers of the Governor and cannot extend to making legislation for the State during the Proclamation or later

questions.explanation: The Court preserved judicial review but at a deferential standard.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A limits the powers wrongly. Option C contradicts S.R. Bommai-type reviewability. Option D adds a condition not mentioned.
questions.clat_trap: Three options sound like constitutional first principles, but only one preserves review with the right standard.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Court's treatment of the reorganisation into Union Territories was that

options.A: Ladakh's creation was struck down and the remainder upheld, since Ladakh has no legislature of its own to be consulted
options.B: both were upheld because Article 3 permits conversion of any State into a Union Territory without limit, whatever the circumstances
options.C: Ladakh's creation was upheld under Article 3, while the rest was left open given the statehood assurance
options.D: both conversions were struck down but their operation was suspended pending legislation by Parliament within a fixed period

questions.explanation: One limb was decided, the other was left open.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option D invent invalidity. Option B overstates by deciding the open question.
questions.clat_trap: A split answer (one part decided, one part left open) is easily collapsed into an all-or-nothing option.
questions.language_trick: 'left open' is a holding in itself.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly records the Court's directions on restoring democratic government?

options.A: Elections were to await the report of a delimitation commission appointed by the Court for the purpose
options.B: Elections by 30 September 2024, and restoration of statehood as soon as possible
options.C: Elections were to be held only after the Ladakh administration had constituted its own legislature
options.D: Statehood was to be restored within six months by a Presidential notification under Article 3

questions.explanation: The directions combined an election deadline with a recorded assurance on statehood.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The remaining options invent timelines or preconditions.
questions.clat_trap: Date-and-detail recall: invented timelines are the standard distractor.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Court upheld the abrogation of Article 370 even though it held the Article 367 route to be impermissible. Reason (R): The President's power under Article 370(3) survived the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly and could independently be exercised.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is accurate and R is the reason the result stood.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R directly explains why the flawed route did not matter.
questions.clat_trap: A looks self-contradictory at first glance and tempts the option 'A is false'.
questions.language_trick: 'even though' signals a concession, not a contradiction.

passages.title: Religious Freedom and the Essential Religious Practices Doctrine
passages.passage: Article 25(1) guarantees to all persons, subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III, freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. Article 25(2)(b) saves laws providing for social welfare and reform, or throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus; Explanation II to Article 25 treats references to Hindus as including persons professing the Sikh, Jain or Buddhist religion. Article 26 gives every religious denomination, subject to public order, morality and health, the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion and to administer its property in accordance with law. Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Shirur Mutt (1954) held that religion includes practices integral to it, to be determined by the religion's own doctrines, and Durgah Committee v. Syed Hussain Ali (1961) added that superstitious accretions are outside protection; the test is whether removal of the practice would fundamentally alter the religion. In Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018), a Bench by 4:1 held that the exclusion of women aged ten to fifty from the Sabarimala temple violated Article 25(1); that worshippers of Lord Ayyappa were not a separate religious denomination, so Article 26 was unavailable; that the exclusion was not essential to Hinduism; and that 'morality' in Articles 25 and 26 means constitutional morality. Justice Indu Malhotra dissented, cautioning against judicial interference in matters of deep religious faith. In November 2019, on review petitions, a Bench by 3:2 did not decide the review on merits but referred wider questions, including the ambit of the essential religious practices doctrine, to a larger Bench; the reference remained pending when this passage was prepared and its status should be verified. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), three of five judges set aside instantaneous triple talaq: two held it manifestly arbitrary under Article 14, while the third held it was not an essential practice and so was unprotected by Article 25.

questions.question: Under the essentiality test as described, a practice is protected under Articles 25 or 26 only if

options.A: it is believed by the majority of the faithful to be obligatory, whatever the doctrine says
options.B: its removal would fundamentally alter the religion, judged by the religion's own doctrines, superstitious accretions being excluded
options.C: it does not conflict with any other provision of the Constitution, including Article 14
options.D: it has been followed without interruption for at least a century

questions.explanation: The test is internal to the religion and asks whether the religion would be fundamentally altered.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A imports a custom-style duration test. Option C replaces doctrine with majority belief. Option D is a condition on all Part III rights and not the essentiality test.
questions.clat_trap: Plausible-sounding tests are offered in place of the doctrinal test.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: In Articles 25 and 26 the word 'morality' was held to mean

options.A: the morality prevailing in public opinion at the relevant time
options.B: the moral standards of the denomination as declared by its religious head
options.C: constitutional morality
options.D: the moral principles enumerated in the Directive Principles alone

questions.explanation: The Sabarimala majority read morality as constitutional morality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is popular morality, which the Court set aside. Option B lets the denomination define the limit on its own rights. Option D narrows the concept without basis.
questions.clat_trap: All three wrong options are things 'morality' could ordinarily mean, so recall of the holding is essential.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The finding that worshippers of Lord Ayyappa were not a religious denomination meant that

options.A: Article 25(2)(b) alone then governed and the exclusion needed no further justification at all
options.B: Article 26 could not justify the exclusion, leaving the claim to be tested under Article 25(1)
options.C: the temple board could still invoke Article 26(d) for administration of the temple
options.D: the temple fell outside Part III and the dispute became purely one of statute and temple custom

questions.explanation: Article 26 belongs to denominations. Without that status the exclusion had to be justified under Article 25(1) alone.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A wrongly removes the temple from constitutional scrutiny. Option C misreads Article 25(2)(b) as a shield. Option D gives a denomination right to a body that is not one.
questions.clat_trap: The consequence of a finding is tested rather than the finding itself.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The November 2019 order on the Sabarimala review petitions is best described as

options.A: an allowance of the review petitions, restoring the earlier exclusion at once
options.B: a recall of the 2018 judgment pending fresh hearing by the same Bench
options.C: a dismissal of the review petitions by a 3:2 majority, affirming the 2018 verdict in full
options.D: a reference of wider questions to a larger Bench, without deciding the reviews on merits

questions.explanation: The Bench left the 2018 judgment standing for now and referred questions to a larger Bench.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats a reference as a dismissal. Option B and Option C assume the 2018 ruling was undone.
questions.clat_trap: A 3:2 split is often misread as a verdict on the merits.
questions.language_trick: 'did not decide ... on merits' is the key phrase, and a reference is not a dismissal.

questions.question: Which statement about Shayara Bano (2017) is accurate on the passage?

options.A: All five judges agreed that the practice was unprotected by Article 25
options.B: Three of five judges set aside the practice, but on two different lines of reasoning
options.C: Three judges held the practice essential to the religion yet struck it down under Article 14
options.D: The Court unanimously held that personal laws are wholly immune from Part III scrutiny

questions.explanation: Two judges relied on manifest arbitrariness and one on non-essentiality, forming a 3:2 majority on different grounds.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the two dissenters. Option C is wrong, as a majority subjected the practice to review. Option D is internally inconsistent with the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A majority outcome with divergent reasoning invites over-simplification into a single ratio.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A State law throwing open a public Sikh gurdwara to all classes of Hindus can fall within Article 25(2)(b). Reason (R): Explanation II to Article 25 treats references to Hindus as including persons professing the Sikh, Jain or Buddhist religion.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Explanation extends 'Hindus' to Sikhs, which is what allows the gurdwara to be treated as a Hindu religious institution.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R supplies the mechanism that makes A work.
questions.clat_trap: A seems offensive to minority sensibilities at first reading, which tempts rejection.
questions.language_trick: 'Hindus' in the Article is a defined, expanded term.

passages.title: Marriage, Identity and Intimate Choice: Navtej, NALSA and Supriyo
passages.passage: In Navtej Singh Johar (2018), a Constitution Bench read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual sexual conduct between adults, holding that sexual orientation is an intrinsic part of identity protected by Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21. The Court overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal and grounded its reasoning in constitutional morality, dignity and autonomy. In NALSA (2014), the Court had earlier recognised the right of transgender persons to self-identify their gender, and directed that they be treated as a socially and educationally backward class for reservations. In Supriyo Chakraborty (2023), a five-judge Bench considered petitions seeking recognition of marriage between same-sex couples. The Bench unanimously held that there is no fundamental right to marry under the Constitution, and that the Special Marriage Act, 1954 could not be read down or have words read into it to include same-sex couples, because the design of the statute, tied to the personal laws, was a matter for Parliament. All five judges accepted that the Court cannot legislate. A majority of three held that there is no right to civil union, while the Chief Justice and Kaul J. would have recognised a duty on the State to confer some legal status on such unions. On adoption, the Chief Justice would have struck down the regulation that excludes unmarried and queer couples from jointly adopting, but the majority upheld the regulation. The Union Government undertook to constitute a committee under the Cabinet Secretary to examine entitlements of queer couples, including ration cards, joint bank accounts and medical decisions.

questions.question: The Supriyo Bench's refusal to read the Special Marriage Act as gender-neutral is best explained by the view that

options.A: the right to marry is a fundamental right but can be exercised only under personal laws
options.B: the Act had already been read down once in Navtej and could not be read down again afterwards
options.C: such a reading would rewrite a statutory scheme that presupposes a man and a woman
options.D: marriage between same-sex partners is a conduct that Section 377 had left criminal

questions.explanation: The Court reasoned that reading words into the Act would be law-making, because its design and its link with personal laws point to a heterosexual union.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is wrong because Navtej decriminalised the conduct. Option B contradicts the holding that there is no fundamental right to marry. Option D invents a history of reading down the Act.
questions.clat_trap: Options that echo Navtej tempt a student who merges the two cases. The distinction is between decriminalisation and positive recognition.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage state as a point of UNANIMITY among the five judges in Supriyo?

options.A: The State has a duty to confer legal status on same-sex unions
options.B: There is no fundamental right to marry and the Court cannot make law
options.C: Queer couples may jointly adopt under the regulation
options.D: The Special Marriage Act is unconstitutional to the extent it excludes them

questions.explanation: The unanimous strands were the absence of a fundamental right to marry and the limit on judicial law-making.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A was supported only by two judges. Option C was the Chief Justice's minority view. Option D was never held by any judge.
questions.clat_trap: A student confuses the minority position with the Bench's position because the Chief Justice authored the lead opinion.
questions.language_trick: 'unanimously' versus 'a majority of three': the stem asks which strand had all five.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Supriyo majority declined to recognise a right to civil union even though it accepted the dignity of queer persons. Reason (R): The Bench held that the Court cannot legislate and that creation of such a status lies with Parliament.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The refusal rested on institutional limits, not on any denial of dignity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R gives the ground on which the majority declined a right to civil union.
questions.clat_trap: Students expect the dignity premise to lead to recognition, so they mark R as unrelated or A as false.
questions.language_trick: 'even though' in A signals a contrast that R explains.

questions.question: Navtej is cited with NALSA for the proposition that

options.A: consensual conduct in private is exempt from regulation by any law whatever
options.B: identity and autonomy, as aspects of dignity, are protected under Article 21
options.C: the State must provide reservation to every sexual minority in education and public employment
options.D: constitutional morality always prevails over a statute's text where the two appear to conflict

questions.explanation: Both decisions rest identity and autonomy on dignity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A extends NALSA's backward-class direction to all groups. Option C is an overstatement because limits like consent remain. Option D uses 'always', which neither decision supports.
questions.clat_trap: Absolute words are the traps in the three wrong options.
questions.language_trick: 'always', 'every' and 'any' signal overstatement.

questions.question: On adoption, the position in the passage is that

options.A: all five judges upheld the regulation excluding queer couples
options.B: the Court left the question entirely undecided
options.C: the Chief Justice would have struck down the exclusion, but the majority upheld it
options.D: the majority struck down the exclusion and the Chief Justice dissented from that holding

questions.explanation: The Chief Justice was in the minority on this issue.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the line-up. Option B ignores the Chief Justice. Option D says there was no decision.
questions.clat_trap: Reversal of the majority and minority is the staple trap.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The recording of the Union's undertaking to constitute a committee is most consistent with the view that

options.A: extending practical entitlements is for the political branches, not for judicial decree
options.B: the Court found the Union's earlier refusal to act to be unconstitutional
options.C: the Court itself had directed the Union to legislate a civil union within a fixed period of one year
options.D: the committee's recommendations would bind the Court in later cases on marriage

questions.explanation: The Court noted the undertaking and left the entitlements to the political branches, in line with its holding that it cannot legislate.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B attributes a mandamus to the Court that it did not issue. Option C makes the executive committee binding on the judiciary. Option D imports a finding that the passage does not contain.
questions.clat_trap: A fact in the passage is dressed up as a legal consequence. Judicial deference is the point of the undertaking, not an order.
questions.language_trick: 'undertook' is a voluntary promise, unlike 'directed'.

passages.title: Article 20: Retroactivity, Double Jeopardy and Self-Incrimination
passages.passage: Article 20 provides three protections to an accused. Clause (1) prohibits conviction for an act that was not an offence at the time it was done, and prohibits a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the offence. It restricts only retrospective criminal law, not retrospective civil liability or procedural change. Clause (2) bars prosecution and punishment more than once for the same offence. The Court has held in Maqbool Hussain that this applies only where the earlier proceeding was a prosecution before a court or judicial tribunal, so that a customs adjudication does not bar a later prosecution. Clause (3) provides that no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. In Selvi (2010), the Court held that involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests violate Article 20(3) and Article 21, though results of voluntary tests may be admitted in a limited manner. In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad, the Court held that compelled production of specimen handwriting or fingerprints is not testimonial compulsion, because the bar covers the conveying of personal knowledge, not the furnishing of physical evidence. The protection applies from the time a person is formally accused, and not before. In Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh the Court held that a law which merely changes the procedure of trial may be applied to offences committed earlier, while an increase in the maximum punishment cannot.

questions.question: A statute enacted in 2024 raises the maximum sentence for an offence from five to seven years. A person who committed the offence in 2022 is tried after the amendment. The Court may impose

options.A: up to seven years, because the trial took place after the amendment
options.B: up to seven years, since sentencing is a matter of procedure and procedure may operate retrospectively
options.C: up to five years, as a heavier penalty than the one then in force is barred
options.D: any term the court thinks fit, since Article 20(1) bars only conviction and not sentence

questions.explanation: The second limb of Article 20(1) bars a penalty greater than that under the law at the time of the offence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A calls sentencing procedural, which the passage rejects. Option B counts the date of trial, which is irrelevant. Option D ignores the second limb.
questions.clat_trap: Procedure may be applied retrospectively, which makes the sentence look procedural.
questions.language_trick: 'maximum punishment' is substantive; the clause turns on the date of the act.

questions.question: A person is fined by a customs officer in an adjudication and is later prosecuted before a Magistrate for the same smuggling. Under the passage, the prosecution is

options.A: barred, because a penalty already paid amounts to punishment
options.B: barred, because the facts and the offence are identical
options.C: barred only if the fine paid was more than half the maximum penalty
options.D: not barred by Article 20(2), because the first proceeding was not a prosecution before a court or judicial tribunal

questions.explanation: Article 20(2) needs prosecution and punishment. A departmental adjudication is not a prosecution before a judicial body.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A focuses only on identity of the offence. Option B ignores the requirement of prosecution. Option C invents a quantum test.
questions.clat_trap: The sameness of the offence is only one element of the bar.
questions.language_trick: 'prosecution' is a term of art. A departmental penalty is not one.

questions.question: Which is NOT a correct application of Article 20(3) as described?

options.A: The protection is available only after the person is formally accused of an offence
options.B: Involuntary narco-analysis of an accused is barred under Article 20(3) and Article 21
options.C: A direction to give fingerprints is unconstitutional for want of cooperation
options.D: Specimen handwriting furnished under compulsion is not testimonial in character

questions.explanation: Fingerprints are physical evidence and not testimonial. The statement in the stem is therefore the incorrect one.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option D state the position correctly.
questions.clat_trap: A negatively worded stem ('NOT') requires picking the incorrect statement, and the correct one appears first as a decoy.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT correct': read the stem twice before marking.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A narco-analysis test conducted with the free consent of the accused cannot be held to violate Article 20(3). Reason (R): The bar in Article 20(3) is on compulsion, and consent removes the compulsion.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court in Selvi allowed voluntary tests subject to safeguards, because Article 20(3) is about compulsion.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states the element that is missing when consent exists.
questions.clat_trap: Students distrust A because of the 'extremely tough' feel of the topic. A simple, direct link holds good.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: X is arrested but formally accused only after he has made a statement under a police summons as a witness. On the passage, the position about that earlier statement is

options.A: that it is wholly inadmissible, because he was later made an accused in the very same case
options.B: that Article 20(3) does not apply, as protection starts only on formal accusation
options.C: that it is protected from the moment of any police suspicion
options.D: that it is admissible only if recorded by a Magistrate

questions.explanation: The protection begins on formal accusation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A extends the protection backwards. Option C adds a requirement from other law. Option D equates suspicion with accusation.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'formally' is essential to the passage's rule.
questions.language_trick: 'formally accused' vs 'suspected'.

questions.question: A new law changes the court that tries an offence committed before the law. The best view under the passage is that

options.A: the law is void under Article 20(1) since it applies retroactively to an act already done before its enactment
options.B: the law can apply only if the new court is a higher court than the one that would earlier have tried the offence
options.C: the law is valid only for offences committed after the date of its enactment and for none committed before that date
options.D: the law may apply to earlier offences, as a change of forum is procedural

questions.explanation: Article 20(1) bars only retrospective criminal liability and heavier penalties.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads the clause as a bar on all retroactivity. Option B repeats that error. Option C adds an unfounded condition.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'retroactively' in the option suggests Article 20(1) but the clause is narrower.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.title: Parliamentary Privileges and the Bribery Exception: From Narasimha Rao to Sita Soren
passages.passage: Articles 105 and 194 confer on members of Parliament and State Legislatures freedom of speech in the House and immunity from court proceedings in respect of anything said or any vote given in the House or any committee. Article 105(3) preserves, until defined by law, the powers, privileges and immunities of the House of Commons as at the commencement of the Constitution. In P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998), a Bench by a majority of three to two held that a Member who had accepted a bribe to vote in a particular way and who did so vote was protected by Article 105(2), as the bribe had a nexus with the vote. In Sita Soren (2024), a seven-judge Bench unanimously overruled that holding. The Court reasoned that the privilege exists to secure the collective functioning of the House and to enable a Member to discharge his functions fearlessly, so a privilege claim must pass the test of being essential to the discharge of a legislator's functions. Bribery is not essential to that function. The offence of bribery is complete when the bribe is accepted, irrespective of whether the promised speech is made or the vote is cast, and so it is not a matter 'in respect of' the vote. The Court added that corruption by members erodes probity in public life and strikes at the foundations of parliamentary democracy. In Raja Ram Pal (2007), the Court held that the exercise of privilege, including the expulsion of members, is open to limited judicial review, and that Article 122 and Article 212 bar the questioning of proceedings on the ground of an irregularity of procedure only. The freedom from arrest that members enjoy is confined to civil matters and does not extend to criminal cases or preventive detention. Whether a Member who is a bribe-giver is also outside the privilege was left to be decided on the same logic, since the privilege is tied to functions and not to persons.

questions.question: The decisive reasoning in Sita Soren for denying immunity to a legislator who takes a bribe for a vote is that

options.A: the offence is complete on acceptance, regardless of whether the vote is later cast, so it is not tied to the vote
options.B: the vote is cast only after a free parliamentary debate and is therefore not open to question in any court of law
options.C: the bribe-taker is liable only if he in fact votes against the party whip after receiving the illegal gratification
options.D: the privilege applies to speech but not to votes under Article 105(2), which deals only with what is spoken in the House

questions.explanation: The Court tied the privilege to what is essential to a legislator's function. Bribery is complete on acceptance, so it stands apart from the vote.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B misstates the logic and supports immunity. Option C brings in the whip, which the passage never mentions. Option D is wrong because Article 105(2) expressly covers votes.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options are shaped like constitutional reasoning, but each rests on a premise absent from the passage.
questions.language_trick: 'regardless of whether' makes the vote irrelevant to the offence.

questions.question: Which statement correctly states the effect of Raja Ram Pal on Article 122 and Article 212?

options.A: They bar every challenge to legislative proceedings, however grave the illegality alleged against them
options.B: They bar a challenge to proceedings but not to the expulsion of any Member
options.C: They bar challenge on procedural irregularity but not on illegality or constitutional violation
options.D: They bar judicial review of a House's decision only when the House is unanimous

questions.explanation: Only irregularity of procedure is shielded. Illegality remains open to limited review.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads the bar as total. Option B invents a condition of unanimity. Option D carves out expulsion, which the passage lists among reviewable acts, but not for the stated reason.
questions.clat_trap: The distinction between irregularity and illegality is the pivot, and the word 'only' in the passage is easy to skip.
questions.language_trick: 'irregularity of procedure only': the bar is narrow.

questions.question: A State legislator is accused of accepting money to put a question in the House. He later puts the question as promised. Under the passage, his claim to immunity under Article 194(2) would

options.A: succeed, because the money was accepted before the session began
options.B: fail, since the offence was complete on acceptance and has no link with the question
options.C: fail only if the question was found to be false or mischievous
options.D: succeed, because the question was in fact put in the House as the member had promised

questions.explanation: The passage treats bribery as complete on acceptance, so the later question does not cloak it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A falls back on the overruled nexus reasoning. Option C adds a timing test not found in the passage. Option D imports a falsity test that is irrelevant.
questions.clat_trap: The overruled Narasimha Rao reasoning is built into one option, which suits students who recall the older rule.
questions.language_trick: 'complete on acceptance' versus 'on performance'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A Member who publishes his own House speech in a pamphlet sold outside enjoys the same immunity as the speech itself. Reason (R): Article 105(2) protects the publication of a report, paper or proceedings by or under the authority of the House.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is true as a statement of the protection given to publication under the authority of the House. A is false because a private republication is outside that authority.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a correct principle but it cuts against A.
questions.clat_trap: R seems to support A because both speak of publication, though R is limited to authorised publication.
questions.language_trick: 'his own' and 'sold outside' mark the departure from authorised publication.

questions.question: The passage presents the purpose of parliamentary privilege primarily as

options.A: preserving the independence of the Speaker from judicial review in every matter arising within the House
options.B: protecting members from criminal prosecution of any kind during a session of the House or its committees
options.C: securing the collective functioning of the House, not the personal advantage of members
options.D: ensuring that no court may examine a member's conduct outside the House where it relates to political activity

questions.explanation: The privilege is functional and collective.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the limit on freedom from arrest. Option B concerns a different office. Option D extends immunity beyond the House.
questions.clat_trap: Option {W1} has the ring of a privilege that many wrongly assume to exist.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A member is arrested on a charge of cheating while the House is in session. On the passage, the arrest is

options.A: not barred by the privilege, since freedom from arrest covers only civil matters
options.B: valid only if the cheating arose from conduct within the House
options.C: valid only if the Speaker has granted prior permission in writing
options.D: barred, since no member may be arrested during a session

questions.explanation: The freedom from arrest is confined to civil matters.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B gives an absolute freedom. Option C states a requirement the passage does not mention. Option D confuses the nexus test with freedom from arrest.
questions.clat_trap: 'during a session' and the idea of 'Speaker's permission' invite a wrong answer based on convention.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.title: The State, Void Laws and Equality: Articles 12, 13 and 14
passages.passage: Article 12 defines the 'State' to include the Government, Parliament, the legislatures and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. In Ajay Hasia (1981) the Court identified indicia for treating a body as an instrumentality of the State, such as State financing, deep and pervasive control, monopoly status and transferred governmental functions. In Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) the Court preferred a broader enquiry, asking whether the body is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by or under the control of the Government, and requiring that the control be 'particular to the body in question' and 'pervasive'. Mere regulation, however strict, does not make a body an instrumentality. Article 13(1) provides that pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void to the extent of the inconsistency, and the Court has held that such laws are not dead but eclipsed, so that they revive if the impediment is removed. Article 13(2) bars the State from making any law that takes away or abridges those rights, and a law so made is void. Article 13(3)(a) includes custom or usage having the force of law. Constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13, but, since Kesavananda Bharati (1973), an amendment is invalid if it destroys the basic structure. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to any person. A classification passes the test if it rests on an intelligible differentia and bears a rational nexus with the object of the law. In E.P. Royappa, arbitrariness was recognised as the antithesis of equality. In Shayara Bano and Navtej the Court has applied manifest arbitrariness to strike down legislation, a view in some tension with the earlier McDowell approach. The guarantee does not enforce equality in illegality: a person cannot claim a benefit just because another was wrongly given one.

questions.question: A privately promoted company that provides data services is 49 per cent financed by public funds, is regulated by a statutory body on tariffs, but is managed by its private board without governmental nominees. Applying Pradeep Kumar Biswas, it is

options.A: the State, because nearly half of its finance comes from public money, which is conclusive
options.B: unlikely to be the State, as part funding and regulation do not show pervasive control
options.C: the State, because its tariffs are subject to a statutory regulator
options.D: the State, because it performs a public function for citizens

questions.explanation: The test needs financial, functional and administrative dominance with pervasive control. Regulation alone does not suffice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats funding as conclusive. Option C treats regulation as control. Option D treats a public-facing service as a governmental function.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option takes a single factor from Ajay Hasia as sufficient, while Pradeep Kumar Biswas requires dominance across the board.
questions.language_trick: 'by themselves' and 'pervasive' are the operative words.

questions.question: A pre-1950 statute is in conflict with a fundamental right at the commencement of the Constitution. On the doctrine of eclipse, the statute

options.A: remains on the book, unenforceable against the right until the bar goes, then revives
options.B: is void from its inception and cannot be revived even by a later constitutional amendment curing the conflict
options.C: is repealed by operation of Article 13(1) and must be re-enacted afresh
options.D: becomes void only for those persons who bring a challenge before a court

questions.explanation: The law is overshadowed, not dead.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies the rule for post-Constitution laws. Option C wrongly makes the voidness depend on a challenge. Option D treats the void as a repeal.
questions.clat_trap: Students commonly mix up Article 13(1) with Article 13(2), where the law is stillborn.
questions.language_trick: 'eclipsed' as against 'dead'.

questions.question: An amendment to the Constitution removes a fundamental right. The correct test of its validity, on the passage, is

options.A: whether it is consistent with custom having the force of law
options.B: whether it abridges a fundamental right, since Article 13(2) applies to it
options.C: whether it destroys the basic structure of the Constitution
options.D: whether it was passed by a two-thirds majority, which concludes its validity

questions.explanation: After Kesavananda, amendments are tested against the basic structure and not by Article 13(2).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats an amendment as law under Article 13(2). Option B makes the special majority conclusive. Option D misapplies Article 13(3)(a).
questions.clat_trap: The tempting answer is Article 13(2), because the stem speaks of removing a right.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Z is wrongly granted a licence in breach of the rules. Y, who is similarly placed, asks the court to direct that he be granted a licence too under Article 14. The court would most likely

options.A: refuse, because Article 14 protects only citizens and not persons
options.B: grant it, but only if Y shows that Z is related to the authority
options.C: refuse, as Article 14 gives no claim to equality in illegality
options.D: grant it, since two similarly situated persons must be treated alike under Article 14

questions.explanation: There is no negative equality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores that the first grant was unlawful. Option B adds an improper condition. Option D misstates Article 14, which applies to persons.
questions.clat_trap: The stem invites a mechanical sameness argument.
questions.language_trick: 'wrongly' signals the illegality.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A classification resting on an intelligible differentia may still violate Article 14. Reason (R): The differentia must also bear a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the law.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A differentia without rational nexus fails Article 14. R states the second limb that explains how A can happen.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R supplies the missing limb of the test.
questions.clat_trap: Students read 'may still' as an exaggeration and reject A.
questions.language_trick: 'still' signals that the first limb is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.question: The passage's treatment of arbitrariness shows that

options.A: Royappa limited arbitrariness to cases where a classification is also made
options.B: the Court has applied manifest arbitrariness to legislation, despite an earlier contrary view
options.C: McDowell has been followed without exception in all later cases
options.D: arbitrariness applies only to executive action and never to a statute, however unreasonable its content may be

questions.explanation: Shayara Bano and Navtej tested statutes, which is in tension with McDowell.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option C contradict the passage. Option D narrows Royappa.
questions.clat_trap: 'Never' and 'without exception' are the absolutes that expose the wrong options.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.title: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: Civil and Criminal Contempt
passages.passage: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 distinguishes civil contempt, which is wilful disobedience of a judgment, decree, direction, order or writ or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court, from criminal contempt, which includes scandalising or lowering the authority of a court, prejudicing or interfering with judicial proceedings, and obstructing the administration of justice. The Supreme Court and the High Courts also hold the power to punish for contempt under Articles 129 and 215. Under Section 12, the punishment is simple imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to two thousand rupees or both, and an explanation provides that an apology shall not be rejected merely because it is qualified or conditional if it is made bona fide. Under Section 13, as amended in 2006, a court shall not punish unless the contempt substantially interferes or tends to substantially interfere with the due course of justice, and truth may be pleaded as a defence if it is in public interest and the request for invoking it is bona fide. Section 3 protects innocent publication or distribution of matter that interferes with proceedings if the publisher had no reasonable grounds to believe that proceedings were pending, and Section 5 provides that fair criticism on the merits of a judicial act, after a case has been heard and finally decided, is not contempt. Under Section 15, in the case of criminal contempt, the court may act on its own motion or on a motion by the Advocate General, or by any other person with his written consent. Section 20 provides that no court shall initiate proceedings after a year has elapsed from the date of the alleged contempt. In Pallav Sheth (2001), the Supreme Court held that proceedings are initiated when the application is made to the court within the year, and not when the court issues notice. In 2020, the Court found a senior advocate guilty of criminal contempt for two tweets and imposed a fine of one rupee, a matter on which critics and supporters of the Court's stance remain divided.

questions.question: An officer knowingly ignores a High Court's direction to release a sum of money to a contractor, who then moves the Court. The conduct is best described as

options.A: no contempt, since the disobedience affects only a private party
options.B: criminal contempt, as it obstructs the administration of justice
options.C: criminal contempt, as it lowers the authority of the court
options.D: civil contempt, as it consists of wilful disobedience of a direction of the court

questions.explanation: Wilful disobedience of a court's direction is civil contempt.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B borrow limbs of criminal contempt, though the conduct falls within the civil limb. Option C overlooks that civil contempt can arise from private wrongs.
questions.clat_trap: Disobedience of an order damages the court's authority, so the criminal label tempts students.
questions.language_trick: 'wilful disobedience' is the textual hook.

questions.question: A columnist alleges that a named judge took a bribe in a decided case, and proves the allegation with documents in good faith and in public interest. On the passage, the columnist

options.A: has a defence only if the case was pending when the article appeared
options.B: may rely on truth as a defence, subject to public interest and bona fides
options.C: has no defence, since truth is no answer to scandalising the court
options.D: may rely on truth only if the judge consents to the inquiry

questions.explanation: After the 2006 amendment, justification by truth is available if the plea is in public interest and the request is bona fide.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the pre-2006 view. Option C invents a consent condition. Option D brings in the pending-case limb.
questions.clat_trap: The old rule that truth is no defence is the common distractor.
questions.language_trick: 'subject to' marks conditions of public interest and bona fides.

questions.question: On 10 January 2025 a person scandalises a court. A petition alleging the contempt is filed on 20 December 2025, and the court issues notice on 15 February 2026. Under the passage, the proceedings are

options.A: barred, because the court must take cognizance within one year of the contempt
options.B: barred by limitation, as notice was issued after one year had already passed from the contempt
options.C: within time only if the delay in issuing notice was caused by the respondent
options.D: within time, as initiation is judged by the date of the application, not of the notice

questions.explanation: Pallav Sheth fixes the date of the application as the date of initiation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A measures the year until notice. Option B reads 'cognizance' instead of 'initiation'. Option C makes the answer depend on who caused the delay.
questions.clat_trap: Dates are arranged so that mechanical counting to the notice yields the wrong answer.
questions.language_trick: 'initiate' and 'take cognizance' are different.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Consent of the Advocate General is a precondition for a court to take up a litigant's complaint of civil contempt. Reason (R): Section 15 requires such consent for a motion by a person other than the Advocate General in the case of criminal contempt.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R correctly states Section 15 as limited to criminal contempt. A extends the consent requirement to civil contempt, which is wrong.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is limited to criminal contempt and so does not support A.
questions.clat_trap: R seems to explain A, but the two concern different types of contempt.
questions.language_trick: 'civil' in A and 'criminal' in R.

questions.question: A contemnor offers an apology that is qualified by a statement that he stands by his criticism. On the passage, the court

options.A: must reject the apology, since a qualified apology is no apology in the eye of the law
options.B: may still accept the apology if bona fide, as qualification alone does not defeat it
options.C: must accept it, as every apology discharges the contemnor
options.D: may accept it only if the Advocate General agrees

questions.explanation: The Explanation to Section 12 forbids rejection merely because the apology is qualified or conditional, but it must be bona fide.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the Explanation. Option C treats acceptance as a right. Option D brings in Section 15 for an unrelated step.
questions.clat_trap: The 'stand by his criticism' detail may suggest insincerity.
questions.language_trick: 'merely' and 'bona fide' are the pivot.

questions.question: A journalist is prosecuted for (i) a balanced critique, after final decision, of a judgment's reasoning and (ii) a headline declaring an accused guilty while his trial is pending. On the passage,

options.A: both are protected as the journalist acted without malice
options.B: the first is contempt and the second is protected as a statement of public interest
options.C: the first is protected as fair criticism of a decided case, while the second may be treated as prejudicing proceedings
options.D: both amount to contempt, as any comment on the judiciary is barred

questions.explanation: Section 5 protects fair criticism of a finally decided case. A pending-trial comment may prejudice proceedings.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the pending-case distinction. Option B bars all comment. Option D reverses the two.
questions.clat_trap: The timing of the comment is the difference between the two acts.
questions.language_trick: 'finally decided' versus 'pending'.

passages.title: Law and Society: Historical, Sociological and Realist Thought
passages.passage: The Historical School, associated with Savigny, held that law is not made by a legislator but grows from the common consciousness of a people, the Volksgeist, and is discovered by jurists. Maine described the movement of progressive societies from status to contract. The Sociological school shifts the focus to the actual workings of law in society. Eugen Ehrlich argued that the centre of gravity of legal development lies not in legislation or juristic science but in society itself, and that the 'living law', the rules by which people actually order their lives, may differ from the law applied by courts. Roscoe Pound described law as social engineering, the ordering of competing individual, public and social interests so as to secure the maximum satisfaction of wants with the minimum of friction and waste. Leon Duguit rejected metaphysical subjective rights and founded law on social solidarity, the interdependence of persons, treating property as a social function that imposes duties on the owner. The American Realists such as Llewellyn and Gray concentrated on what officials and courts actually do, and Jerome Frank, a fact-skeptic, argued that uncertainty arises less from vague rules than from the unpredictable finding of facts by trial courts, a point of difference with rule-skeptics who attack the certainty of rules themselves. Critics of Pound say that the interests he lists give no principle for ranking them in a conflict. Critics of Ehrlich ask how living law is to be distinguished from social habit that has no legal quality. The Realists have been accused of describing law as a prediction of judicial behaviour while neglecting the normative aspect of law, though they insist that the study of what courts do is a necessary step in understanding law.

questions.question: A village follows an unwritten rule of grazing rights, while the official land code says nothing about it. An Ehrlich-style scholar would say that

options.A: without any legal quality until a legislature enacts it into a statute that the courts can apply to the dispute
options.B: valid only if the Volksgeist of the whole nation, and not merely that of the village, approves of its content
options.C: the village rule is living law and may govern conduct even though the courts and statute book do not state it
options.D: part of law only if a court has enforced it by sanction in an earlier case between members of the village

questions.explanation: Ehrlich treated the rules actually followed in society as the real law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option D adopt the positivist idea that law derives from the State. Option B merges Ehrlich with Savigny.
questions.clat_trap: The mixture of Savigny's national spirit with Ehrlich is a test of the exact view.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which pairing of thinker and idea is INCORRECT on the passage?

options.A: Ehrlich: law is the command of a sovereign backed by sanction
options.B: Savigny: law grows from the common consciousness of a people
options.C: Pound: law is the ordering of competing interests with minimum friction
options.D: Duguit: property is a social function imposing duties on the owner

questions.explanation: Law as a sovereign's command is Austin's view and not Ehrlich's.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are accurately matched.
questions.clat_trap: The stem asks for the incorrect pairing, which appears among three correct ones.
questions.language_trick: 'INCORRECT' reverses the usual selection habit.

questions.question: Jerome Frank's fact-skepticism differs from rule-skepticism in that it

options.A: holds that judges decide cases solely on the basis of binding precedent and statute text
options.B: locates the uncertainty in the vagueness of legislative language and the variety of precedents
options.C: denies that any rules exist and treats statutes as meaningless in judicial decision-making
options.D: locates the uncertainty mainly in how trial courts find the facts

questions.explanation: Fact-skeptics emphasise the uncertainty of fact-finding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates the Realists. Option B contradicts the realist view of what judges do. Option C states the rule-skeptic's claim.
questions.clat_trap: The third option borrows the rule-skeptic's idea and presents it as fact-skepticism.
questions.language_trick: 'fact' versus 'rule' is the whole contrast.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Under Duguit's theory, ownership of a factory may be limited by duties to the community. Reason (R): Duguit based law on social solidarity and rejected metaphysical subjective rights.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: If rights are not metaphysical and law rests on interdependence, property carries social duties.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R supplies the premise from which A follows.
questions.clat_trap: Students link property with natural rights and so reject A.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A common criticism of Pound's theory is that

options.A: it treats law as a command that need not reflect any social interest at all
options.B: it confines law to the customs of the past and rejects reform
options.C: it denies that courts have any role in balancing claims
options.D: it lists interests but gives no principle for ranking them in conflict

questions.explanation: The passage records the ranking objection.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A describes Austin. Option B contradicts Pound. Option C describes the Historical School.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options attribute to Pound the features of other schools.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Realist emphasis on what courts actually do is, according to the passage, said by critics to

options.A: treat the law as unchanging, a charge that the Realists reject
options.B: neglect the normative side of law, while Realists reply that studying behaviour is a necessary step
options.C: deny that judges ever apply rules at all, a charge that the Realists accept as accurate on the whole
options.D: rely wholly on legislation, a charge that the Realists accept as fair

questions.explanation: The passage records both the critique and the reply.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives an inaccurate response. Option C invents a charge. Option D inverts the Realist position.
questions.clat_trap: Both the criticism and the reply must be right, so that a half-correct option is wrong.
questions.language_trick: 'necessary step' qualifies the Realists' reply.

passages.title: Possession, Custody, Finders and Possessory Remedies
passages.passage: Possession involves a physical element, effective control, and a mental element, the intention to hold the thing for oneself. A servant who holds his master's tools has mere custody, so that possession remains with the master. A bailee has possession but not ownership. Ownership is the residuary and most extensive right over a thing, including the right to possess, use and dispose of it. At common law, a finder of a lost chattel acquires a title good against everyone except the true owner, as in Armory v. Delamirie, where a chimney sweep's boy prevailed against a goldsmith who kept the jewel. Where the object is found embedded in the land or attached to it, the occupier of the land has a stronger claim, as in South Staffordshire Water Co. v. Sharman, while a thing found on the floor of the public part of a shop belongs to the finder as against the shopkeeper, as in Bridges v. Hawkesworth. Under Section 168 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a finder may sue the owner for any specific reward offered and retain the goods until he receives it, while Section 169 allows him to sell the goods if the owner cannot with reasonable diligence be found, or refuses to pay lawful charges, or if the lawful charges amount to two-thirds of the value of the goods, or if the thing is perishable. Under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a person dispossessed of immovable property without his consent, otherwise than in due course of law, may recover possession by a suit instituted within six months, without proof of title. In such a suit, the defendant cannot set up title as a defence, but either party may sue on title afterward. A pledgee holds possession of the pledged goods, with a special property, while the pledgor retains general ownership and the right of redemption.

questions.question: A shop assistant is given a cash tray to hold during his shift and is told to hand it over at closing. In legal analysis, as between him and the shop owner, he has

options.A: possession as a bailee, since he undertook to return it
options.B: ownership, since money passes by mere delivery
options.C: custody only, with possession remaining in the owner
options.D: possession, since he has physical control of the money

questions.explanation: A servant holding for his master has mere custody.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A focuses on the physical element alone. Option B confuses the passing of money with the passing of ownership. Option D treats a servant like a bailee.
questions.clat_trap: Physical control suggests possession, and the contrast between possession and custody is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'mere custody' is a technical expression.

questions.question: A farm labourer, digging a drain on a landowner's private field, finds a cache of old gold coins embedded in the soil. As between the two, the stronger claim, on the passage, lies with

options.A: the landowner as occupier, because the coins were embedded in his land
options.B: the labourer, as the first person to take the coins into his hand and to exercise control over them after the discovery
options.C: the labourer, because the owner of the coins is unknown and the finder has the best title against everyone else
options.D: the State, because the coins have no known owner and treasure of that kind is taken to belong to the sovereign

questions.explanation: For objects embedded in land, the occupier has the stronger claim (Sharman).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B and Option C apply the general finder's rule. Option D brings in treasure laws that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: Armory suggests the finder wins in all cases, and the embedded position is the exception.
questions.language_trick: 'embedded' directs the analysis to Sharman.

questions.question: A finder holds a lost consignment of goods and the owner is located. The lawful charges of the finder now equal two-thirds of the goods' value, and the owner refuses to pay. Under Section 169, the finder

options.A: must go to court for permission before any sale of the goods can take place
options.B: may sell only if the owner cannot be found with reasonable diligence despite inquiries
options.C: may sell, as lawful charges amount to two-thirds of the value
options.D: may sell only if the goods are perishable or likely to lose the greater part of their value

questions.explanation: Section 169 permits sale where the lawful charges amount to two-thirds of the value of the goods.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds a requirement. Option B and Option D pick one ground when the section lists several, and the stem is satisfied by another.
questions.clat_trap: The grounds in Section 169 are alternatives, so a student who fixes on one will mark a wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'or' links the four grounds.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In a Section 6 suit, a defendant who is the true owner of the property cannot defeat the plaintiff by proving his title. Reason (R): Such a suit concerns possession and not title, and either party may later sue on title.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Section 6 protects peaceful possession, and title is left to a separate suit. R gives the reason for A.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R explains why title cannot be set up.
questions.clat_trap: Students feel that a true owner must win, and so mark A false.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A pledgee of jewellery has it stolen by a stranger. On the passage, the pledgee

options.A: can sue the thief, as possession with special property is good title against a wrongdoer
options.B: cannot sue, because only the pledgor as owner can sue for the theft of the pledged goods held by him
options.C: cannot sue, since a pledgee has no interest in the goods
options.D: can sue only after exercising the right of redemption

questions.explanation: Possession is enough against a wrongdoer.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B gives the right to the owner alone. Option C denies the special property. Option D misplaces the right of redemption, which belongs to the pledgor.
questions.clat_trap: Ownership and possession are separate, and the wrong options assume only the owner can sue.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A tenant is forcibly evicted by the owner without a court order, and files a suit eight months later seeking to recover possession under Section 6. The suit is

options.A: barred, since the owner's title defeats a claim to possession brought by a mere tenant
options.B: maintainable, but only if the tenant first proves his title to the premises in the suit
options.C: maintainable, since the eviction was without due process of law and he was dispossessed forcibly
options.D: barred, as the six-month limit has expired

questions.explanation: A Section 6 suit must be filed within six months of dispossession.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the time limit. Option B requires proof of title, which is unnecessary. Option C allows title to be set up, which the section forbids.
questions.clat_trap: The unlawful eviction makes students ignore the time bar.
questions.language_trick: 'within six months' is a condition and not a technicality.

passages.title: Law and Morality: The Hart-Devlin and Hart-Fuller Debates
