passages.passage: The relationship between law and morality has been debated most sharply in the Hart-Devlin controversy that followed the Wolfenden Report (1957), which recommended that consensual homosexual conduct between adults in private should no longer be a crime. Lord Devlin argued that a society is held together by a shared morality, and that conduct violating that morality may be punished because its toleration threatens the society itself, as treason threatens a government. The legislator, in his view, should ascertain the judgment of the reasonable man or the man in the jury box, whose marks are intolerance, indignation and disgust. H. L. A. Hart, following J. S. Mill's harm principle, replied that the claim that deviation from shared morality leads to social disintegration is an empirical assertion for which Devlin gave no evidence. Hart also distinguished positive morality, meaning the morality actually accepted and shared by a social group, from critical morality, meaning the general moral principles used to criticise social institutions, including positive morality. To enforce the former merely because it is widely held, he said, is to confuse the existence of a moral view with its justification. In Shaw v. Director of Public Prosecutions (1962) the House of Lords upheld a conviction for conspiracy to corrupt public morals, and Viscount Simonds spoke of the court as the guardian of public morals; the decision is often cited as an example of the reasoning Devlin favoured. A separate debate arose between Hart and Lon Fuller over the grudge informer case, in which a post-war German court punished a woman who had denounced her husband under a Nazi statute. Hart took the view that the statute was valid law though morally evil, and that the proper response was to say that it was law but too wicked to obey. Fuller argued that law has an inner morality of eight desiderata: generality, promulgation, prospectivity, clarity, consistency, possibility of compliance, constancy through time and congruence between declared rule and official action. A system that flagrantly fails these, he contended, is not law in the full sense and the statute deserved no recognition. Hart replied that these are principles of efficiency, like the principles of a successful poisoner's craft, and not principles of morality.

questions.question: Devlin's defence of enforcing morality by law rests mainly on the claim that

options.A: criminal law should be confined to conduct that causes harm to persons other than the actor
options.B: conduct that offends moral sentiment always inflicts a measurable harm on identifiable individuals within society
options.C: a society's shared morality is a bond whose breach may threaten its existence
options.D: individual conscience, rather than community opinion, is the proper standard for the legislator to follow

questions.explanation: Devlin's thesis is that shared morality is part of the cement of society, so its breach can threaten the society's existence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A describes a harm-based view that Devlin did not rely on. Option B puts individual conscience above the community standard, the opposite of his reasoning. Option D is the Mill-Hart harm principle, which Devlin rejected.
questions.clat_trap: Two of the wrong options are Hart's side of the debate, so a student who mixes up the two jurists is drawn to them.
questions.language_trick: 'Shared morality' and 'bond' point to Devlin, whereas 'harm' points to Hart.

questions.question: Hart's primary objection to Devlin's disintegration thesis was that it

options.A: confuses the task of the legislator with the task of the judge applying a statute
options.B: presents as established fact a sociological prediction for which no evidence was offered
options.C: wrongly assumes that any society can survive without a shared moral code at all, even for a short time
options.D: relies on Mill's harm principle, which Hart regarded as discredited

questions.explanation: Hart treated the disintegration claim as an empirical hypothesis that Devlin asserted without proof.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attributes to Hart a denial he did not make, since he accepted that some shared morality exists. Option C brings in a legislator-judge split that is not in the passage. Option D reverses Hart's attitude to Mill, whose principle he followed.
questions.clat_trap: Options that sound jurisprudentially sophisticated attract students who have not noticed that the objection was about evidence.
questions.language_trick: 'Empirical' versus 'conceptual': the objection concerns the lack of evidence, not a flaw of logic.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among Fuller's eight desiderata of the inner morality of law, as listed in the passage?

options.A: constancy of the rules through time, so that they are not changed so often that orientation is lost
options.B: conformity with the community's positive morality
options.C: possibility of compliance by those governed, so that no one is commanded to do the impossible
options.D: congruence between declared rules and the actual administration of them by officials

questions.explanation: Fuller's eight are generality, promulgation, prospectivity, clarity, consistency, possibility of compliance, constancy and congruence. Agreement with community morality is not among them.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D are each one of the eight desiderata in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A NOT-type stem with three true items and one false one. The phrase 'inner morality' tempts students to believe that law must match community morals, so the false item looks natural.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' reverses the usual task: the odd one out is the plausible 'morality' item.

questions.question: Consider the following statements about the Hart-Fuller debate as presented in the passage. 1. Hart treated the Nazi informer statute as valid law though morally evil. 2. Fuller maintained that a system flagrantly lacking inner morality does not deserve the name of law. 3. Hart regarded Fuller's eight principles as principles of efficiency and not of morality. 4. Hart and Fuller agreed that the statute was valid law. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1, 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1 and 4 only
options.C: 2, 3 and 4 only

questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are as stated in the passage. Statement 4 is wrong because Fuller denied that the statute deserved recognition as law, so the two did not agree.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B pairs a true statement with the false fourth one and omits two true ones. Option C includes the false fourth statement and drops statement 1. Option D fails because of statement 4.
questions.clat_trap: Statement 4 reads like a harmless compromise, which tempts students who recall only that the informer was punished.
questions.language_trick: 'Agreed' is a universal claim about two jurists whose debate was built on their disagreement.

questions.question: Shaw v. Director of Public Prosecutions is cited as an illustration of Devlin's approach because the House of Lords

options.A: applied a statute that expressly defined an offence of conspiring to corrupt public morals
options.B: left the matter to Parliament on the ground that morality lies outside criminal law
options.C: treated protection of public morals as a proper object of criminal liability
options.D: required proof of harm to a specific, identifiable victim before holding the conduct criminal

questions.explanation: The Lords accepted a residual power to punish conspiracy to corrupt public morals, which matches Devlin's view that law may protect shared morality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the harm-based test that Hart supported. Option B is contrary to the decision. Option D is wrong because the offence was a creation of the common law and not of an express statute.
questions.clat_trap: A student who remembers Shaw as a controversial decision may pick the 'harm' option as a criticism. The stem asks why it is cited, not whether it is approved.
questions.language_trick: 'Cited as an illustration' tests the link to Devlin, not approval of the decision.

questions.question: The distinction between positive and critical morality supports Hart's argument by showing that Devlin

options.A: equates critical morality with whatever the jury's majority happens to accept
options.B: restricts legal enforcement to moral views that survive critical scrutiny
options.C: denies that a pluralist society can have any positive morality at all, whatever its composition
options.D: treats a morality's being widely held as enough to justify enforcing it

questions.explanation: Hart's point is that Devlin treats positive morality as self-justifying and never asks whether it passes the test of critical morality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A says Devlin denied positive morality, whereas he relied on it. Option B mislabels the jury's view, which is positive morality, as critical morality. Option C describes Hart's own position, not Devlin's.
questions.clat_trap: The last wrong option is true of Hart. The stem asks what the distinction shows about Devlin.
questions.language_trick: 'Shows that Devlin' fixes the subject as Devlin, not Hart.

passages.title: The Right of Private Defence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from 1 July 2024, retains the substance of the law of private defence. Every person has a right, subject to restrictions, to defend his own body and the body of any other person, and the property, movable or immovable, of himself or of any other person, against specified offences. The right is preventive and not punitive. It begins when a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body or property arises, even though the offence has not yet been committed, and it continues only as long as that apprehension continues. In the case of offences against the body, the right extends to voluntarily causing death where the assault reasonably causes apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, kidnapping, acid attack and certain other grave offences. In the case of property, it extends to causing death only where the offence is robbery, house-breaking by night, arson of a dwelling, or theft, mischief or house-trespass under circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt. In every other case the right extends only to causing harm other than death. The right does not exist where there is time to have recourse to public authorities, and it never extends to inflicting more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence. There is no right of private defence against an act done or attempted by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of his office, though the act may not be strictly justifiable by law, unless the act causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. The right is available even against an act that would be an offence but for the youth, immaturity or unsoundness of mind of the doer. The accused need not specifically plead private defence and the court may infer it from the record, but where he relies upon it the burden of establishing it lies on him, which he may discharge by showing a preponderance of probabilities. A person who exceeds the right in good faith, without premeditation and without intending to do more harm than necessary, and thereby causes death, is guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

questions.question: A is assaulted by B with a stick. After A's hand is broken, B throws away the stick and runs off. A runs after B and strikes him with an iron rod, fracturing his arm. A's plea of private defence will probably fail because

options.A: the right is preventive, and it ended once the apprehension of further danger ceased
options.B: the right to defend the body never extends to causing hurt in return for hurt
options.C: A used a weapon different from the one that B had used in the assault
options.D: A had time to approach the public authorities, so the right never arose

questions.explanation: The right lasts only as long as the reasonable apprehension of danger. When B threw down the stick and fled, the danger ended and A's act became retaliation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is an overstatement, as the right can extend to causing hurt while the danger lasts. Option C is wrong because A had no time to approach authorities when the assault began. Option D imports a requirement of matching weapons that the law does not have.
questions.clat_trap: The initial attack makes the whole sequence look like defence. The question is about the moment at which the right ends.
questions.language_trick: 'After A's hand is broken' and 'runs off' mark the point at which the danger ended.

questions.question: At night X sees a thief carrying away a bicycle from his courtyard and, though not apprehending any hurt, shoots him dead. On the passage X

options.A: may cause death because the right of property continues until the property is recovered
options.B: may cause death, as the thief entered the dwelling premises at night and so threatened the household
options.C: is not entitled to cause death, as simple theft stops short of it
options.D: may cause death only if the bicycle's value exceeds a prescribed amount

questions.explanation: For theft the right extends to death only where there is reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. X had none, so he could cause only lesser harm.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses theft from a courtyard with house-breaking by night. Option B invents a value threshold. Option D is a half-truth: the right may continue until recovery, but its extent is still limited by the nature of the offence.
questions.clat_trap: 'At night' and 'continues until recovery' echo real rules and so invite a wrong match.
questions.language_trick: 'Though not apprehending any hurt' removes the one fact that would have extended the right to death.

questions.question: A police constable, acting in good faith under colour of his office, arrests Y without a warrant in a case where the arrest is not legally justified, using no more force than ordinary handcuffing. Y pushes him away and escapes. On the passage

options.A: Y cannot plead it only if the constable had displayed a warrant at the time of arrest, otherwise he can in every case
options.B: Y can plead it if he reasonably believed that the arrest was a mere pretext for harassing him in the presence of others
options.C: Y cannot plead it, as the constable acted in good faith and no fear of death or grievous hurt arose
options.D: Y can plead it, because every illegal arrest gives rise to a right of private defence against the person arresting

questions.explanation: The right is barred against a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office, even where the act is not strictly justifiable, unless it causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the exception. Option B replaces the objective test of good faith with the arrested person's belief. Option D makes the bar depend on a warrant, which is not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'illegal' tempts students to assume that resisting an illegal arrest is always permitted.
questions.language_trick: 'Not strictly justifiable' is different from 'mala fide', and the exception covers the former.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the accused's position on private defence at trial, as described in the passage?

options.A: He need not have pleaded it expressly, but must establish it on a preponderance of probabilities
options.B: He must have pleaded it expressly, and he must prove it beyond reasonable doubt like any other exception to liability
options.C: He need not plead it and need not prove it, since the prosecution must in every case negate it by its own evidence
options.D: He must have pleaded it expressly, after which the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt at the trial

questions.explanation: The court may infer the plea from the record, and the burden on the accused is the lighter civil standard.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B raises both the pleading requirement and the standard. Option C shifts the burden to the prosecution. Option D removes the burden from the accused altogether.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option changes one of two variables, pleading and standard, so a student who remembers only one half is drawn to them.
questions.language_trick: 'Need not have pleaded' and 'preponderance' are the two exact phrases that decide the answer.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. The right of private defence begins on reasonable apprehension of danger, even before the offence is committed. 2. The right may be exercised even where there was ample time to seek the protection of public authorities. 3. The right never extends to inflicting more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence. 4. The right is available even against an act that would be an offence but for the unsoundness of mind of the doer. Which statements are correct?

options.A: 1, 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1, 3 and 4 only
options.C: 2 and 4 only

questions.explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 follow the passage. Statement 2 is wrong because the right does not exist where there is time to have recourse to public authorities.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes the false statement 2 and omits 4. Option C includes statement 2 and omits 1 and 3. Option D fails because of statement 2.
questions.clat_trap: Statement 4 sounds odd, since an insane person commits no offence, so some students reject it and the correct option with it.
questions.language_trick: 'Even where' in statement 2 is the language marker of an overstatement.

questions.question: A, in genuine fear of death, strikes B with a heavy rod and kills him. The court finds that one blow was more than necessary, but that A acted without premeditation and without intending more harm than necessary. A is guilty of

options.A: causing death by negligence, because the excess was unintended and without malice
options.B: culpable homicide not amounting to murder
options.C: no offence, because he acted under a reasonable apprehension of death to himself
options.D: murder, because any excess over the right of private defence destroys the defence altogether

questions.explanation: The passage provides that excess of the right, in good faith and without premeditation, reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the exception for good-faith excess. Option C treats the excess as irrelevant. Option D mislabels the offence as negligence, whereas the act was a voluntary blow.
questions.clat_trap: The stem starts with 'genuine fear of death', which tempts a complete-acquittal answer. The finding of 'one blow more than necessary' is what changes the result.
questions.language_trick: 'More than necessary' signals excess; 'in good faith' signals the exception.

passages.title: Offences against Property: Theft, Extortion, Robbery, Cheating and Breach of Trust
passages.passage: Offences against property under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 follow the structure of the Indian Penal Code with some additions, including the separate offence of snatching. Theft is committed by one who, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking. Dishonestly means with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another. Immovable property cannot be stolen, but a thing attached to the earth becomes movable once it is severed. Possession, not ownership, is the test, so an owner can commit theft of his own property if it is in the lawful possession of another, for example a pledgee. A bona fide claim of right, even if mistaken, negates dishonest intention. Extortion requires that the offender intentionally puts a person in fear of injury to that person or another, and thereby dishonestly induces the person to deliver property. Robbery is theft or extortion accompanied by, or involving, instant death, hurt or wrongful restraint or fear thereof; in extortion-robbery the fear must be of instant harm. Dacoity is robbery committed or attempted by five or more persons conjointly. Cheating requires deception which fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver property or do something he would not otherwise do. Criminal breach of trust requires entrustment of property, or dominion over it, and a dishonest misappropriation or conversion of it in violation of a direction of law or contract. The distinction between cheating and criminal breach of trust is that in the former the dishonest intention exists at the inception and induces the delivery, whereas in the latter the owner parts with the property voluntarily and the dishonest intention arises later. In Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) the Supreme Court explained that a mere breach of contract cannot give rise to a prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown at the time of making the promise.

questions.question: A pledges his watch with Z for a loan. Without repaying the loan, A secretly takes the watch from Z's shelf intending to deprive Z of his security. Under the passage A has

options.A: committed no offence, because a person cannot commit theft of his own property, whatever the pledge
options.B: committed criminal breach of trust, because the pledge created a relationship of trust between them
options.C: committed cheating, because A deceived Z about his intention to repay the loan
options.D: committed theft, because possession was with Z and the taking was dishonest

questions.explanation: Possession, not ownership, is the test. The watch was in Z's lawful possession, and A's taking caused Z wrongful loss of his security.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the possession test. Option B wrongly treats the pledgee's holding as entrustment by A to himself. Option C invents a deception that the facts do not contain.
questions.clat_trap: The ownership of the watch makes the act feel innocent. The passage's example of a pledgee is the key to the question.
questions.language_trick: 'Secretly takes' and 'his security' point to dishonest intent and Z's possession.

questions.question: R threatens S: 'Pay me Rs 50,000 or I will accuse you tomorrow of a crime you did not commit.' S pays him at once. R has committed

options.A: robbery, since S delivered the money immediately after the threat was made
options.B: theft, since S paid under pressure and so did not give a free consent
options.C: cheating, since S was deceived about R's real intention to accuse him
options.D: extortion, as the fear was of future injury

questions.explanation: The threat concerns an injury to reputation in future. Robbery by extortion requires fear of instant harm, so the offence stays as extortion.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats the speed of payment as the test, whereas the test is the nature of the fear. Option B confuses extortion with theft. Option C wrongly searches for deception in what was a threat.
questions.clat_trap: The immediacy of payment pulls students towards robbery. The relevant immediacy is that of the threatened harm.
questions.language_trick: 'Tomorrow' is the word that rules out instant harm.

questions.question: A commission agent receives goods from his principal for sale and, after selling them, keeps the price for himself. The offence is

options.A: theft, since the sale price was taken out of the principal's possession without his consent after the sale was completed
options.B: criminal breach of trust, since the goods were entrusted and later dishonestly converted
options.C: extortion, since the principal was induced to part with the goods through a fear of injury put to him by the agent
options.D: cheating, since the agent obtained the goods from the principal by deceiving him at the time of entrustment

questions.explanation: The principal voluntarily entrusted the goods, and the dishonest misappropriation came later. This is the pattern of criminal breach of trust.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overlooks that the agent had the goods by entrustment. Option C requires deception at inception, which is not stated. Option D requires fear of injury, which is absent.
questions.clat_trap: Both cheating and breach of trust involve dishonesty about another's property, which makes a quick reader choose cheating.
questions.language_trick: 'Receives' and 'after selling' fix the order: entrustment first, dishonesty later.

questions.question: A company agrees to supply machinery to B against advance payment, takes the money and, because of financial trouble, does not deliver. No evidence shows dishonest intention when the promise was made. On the passage

options.A: the company is guilty of criminal breach of trust, as the advance was entrusted to it
options.B: the company is guilty of theft, as it kept B's money without his continuing consent
options.C: the dispute is civil, as dishonest intention at inception is missing
options.D: the company is guilty of cheating, as the advance was obtained by a promise it later broke

questions.explanation: Hridaya Ranjan requires dishonest intention at the time of making the promise. Without it, a breach of contract is only a civil wrong.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A equates a broken promise with cheating. Option B treats an advance payment of price as entrustment. Option D overlooks that B delivered the money voluntarily.
questions.clat_trap: Students trained on criminal outcomes assume that a victim who lost money must have a criminal remedy.
questions.language_trick: 'No evidence' and 'when the promise was made' fix the time at which the intention must be tested.

questions.question: P, believing in good faith that a field belongs to him, harvests the standing crop, which in fact belongs to Q, who is in possession. P

options.A: no offence, since a standing crop is immovable property and cannot be the subject of theft before it is severed
options.B: theft, because severance made the crop movable and the intention of the taker is then wholly irrelevant
options.C: theft, since the crop belonged to Q, who was in possession and did not consent to its removal by P
options.D: has not committed theft, since a bona fide claim of right, though mistaken, negates dishonest intention

questions.explanation: A bona fide claim of right negates dishonesty. Severance makes the crop movable, but theft still needs dishonest intention, which P lacked.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the claim of right. Option B is partly true as to standing crops but wrong in this case since severance happened, and it gives the wrong reason. Option C wrongly makes intention irrelevant.
questions.clat_trap: The option on immovable property is a half-truth that appeals to students who recall the severance rule. The reason, not the label, is what decides the answer.
questions.language_trick: 'In good faith' and 'though mistaken' are the phrases that settle the question.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Dacoity requires five or more persons conjointly committing or attempting robbery. 2. Robbery is an aggravated form of theft or extortion. 3. Dishonest intention at the time of taking is an essential ingredient of theft. 4. A standing tree can be the subject of theft without being severed from the earth. Which statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 4 only
options.B: 2, 3 and 4 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3 only

questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 follow the passage. Statement 4 is wrong because a thing attached to the earth becomes movable, and so the subject of theft, only on severance.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement 4 and omits two true statements. Option B includes statement 4 and drops statement 1. Option C fails because of statement 4.
questions.clat_trap: The fourth statement sounds like a technical refinement, which attracts students who recall that trees are property.
questions.language_trick: 'Without being severed' is the phrase that makes the statement false.

passages.title: BNSS: Inherent Powers, Cognizance, Summoning and Recall of Witnesses
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure with effect from 1 July 2024, preserves the inherent powers of the High Court to give effect to orders under the Sanhita, to prevent abuse of the process of any court, and otherwise to secure the ends of justice. In State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992) the Supreme Court listed illustrative categories in which a First Information Report or complaint may be quashed, for instance where the allegations, even if taken at face value and accepted in their entirety, disclose no offence, or where the proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides. The power is to be exercised sparingly, and the High Court does not hold a mini-trial or enquire into the reliability of the allegations at that stage. In Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012) and later cases the Court held that proceedings arising from non-compoundable offences of a predominantly private or civil character may be quashed on settlement, but not those for heinous offences such as murder or rape. A Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, not of an offender, when he applies his mind to the material with a view to proceeding judicially, and he may therefore summon persons not named in a police report if the material discloses their complicity. Under the provision of the BNSS corresponding to Section 319 of the Code, the Constitution Bench in Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab (2014) held that the court may proceed against a person who appears from the evidence recorded at trial to be involved, that such evidence may be the examination-in-chief and need not await cross-examination, and that the satisfaction required is stronger than a prima facie case at the stage of framing charge, though short of that required for conviction. The power to summon a witness, or to recall one already examined, in the provision corresponding to Section 311 of the Code, may be exercised at any stage of an inquiry, trial or other proceeding. The text states that the court 'may' summon or examine, but that it 'shall' summon or recall if the evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case. The power is not to be used to fill a lacuna in the prosecution case where this would prejudice the accused.

questions.question: 'Cognizance', as described in the passage, means

options.A: the Magistrate's judicial application of mind to the offence, rather than to named offenders
options.B: the framing of charges against the persons named in the police report
options.C: the Magistrate's satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt that the offender committed the offence
options.D: the registration of the First Information Report by the officer in charge of the police station

questions.explanation: Cognizance is taken of the offence, and it is the application of judicial mind to the material that constitutes it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B describes a police step. Option C describes a later stage. Option D states a standard of proof used only at the end of the trial.
questions.clat_trap: The phrase 'taking cognizance' is often loosely used for any initiation of the case, which leads to confusion with registration or charge.
questions.language_trick: 'Of the offence, not of an offender' is the passage's own phrase.

questions.question: The standard of satisfaction for summoning an additional accused, as set out in Hardeep Singh, is

options.A: proof beyond reasonable doubt of the person's complicity, drawn from the evidence led at trial
options.B: above the prima facie standard, but below that needed to convict
options.C: the same prima facie standard that applies when charges are framed
options.D: the Magistrate's subjective belief, with no need to rest on evidence recorded at trial

questions.explanation: The Constitution Bench placed the test above a prima facie case but below the level required for conviction.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A understates the test. Option C overstates it. Option D removes the requirement of evidence recorded at trial.
questions.clat_trap: Students recall 'prima facie' from the charge stage and carry it over to the summoning stage.
questions.language_trick: 'Stronger than ... though short of' describes a middle standard, and both ends are decoys.

questions.question: A person accused in an FIR asks the High Court to quash it, producing documents that support his version of the events. The High Court should

options.A: hold a limited trial on the documents to see whether the FIR is genuine
options.B: dismiss the petition, since the High Court has no power to interfere before charge is framed
options.C: ordinarily decline to weigh defence material, and test only whether the allegations disclose an offence
options.D: quash the FIR at once if, on a comparison of both sides' papers, the defence version appears the more probable one

questions.explanation: At the quashing stage the allegations are taken at face value and there is no mini-trial.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invites a weighing of probabilities that the passage excludes. Option B denies the power altogether. Option D describes a mini-trial.
questions.clat_trap: The accused's documents seem persuasive, and a student may think that the court must look at them in the interest of justice.
questions.language_trick: 'Ordinarily' signals that exceptions exist, but not on the facts given.

questions.question: After the prosecution has closed its evidence, the prosecutor finds that the investigating officer was never asked to identify the weapon and applies to recall him. The court should

options.A: refuse, since a witness once examined cannot be recalled in any circumstance after the evidence is closed
options.B: allow, since the power to recall can be exercised at any stage of the trial and is entirely unqualified
options.C: allow only if the defence consents to the recall and the court records that the accused will suffer no prejudice
options.D: refuse if the sole purpose is to fill that gap to the prejudice of the accused, even though the power is wide

questions.explanation: The power is wide but not meant to fill a lacuna in the prosecution case where that would prejudice the accused.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overlooks the limit on the power. Option B denies the power of recall. Option C makes the power depend on consent.
questions.clat_trap: 'At any stage' sounds unlimited. The limit lies in the purpose of the application.
questions.language_trick: 'Sole purpose' and 'prejudice' are the words that narrow the answer.

questions.question: On the text of the provision on summoning or recalling witnesses, the best account is that

options.A: the court has discretion throughout and may refuse even when evidence appears essential
options.B: the court may summon only on the prosecution's request and only before arguments commence
options.C: the provision is mandatory throughout and the court must grant every application by either side
options.D: a general discretion applies, but once the evidence appears essential to a just decision the duty becomes mandatory

questions.explanation: The first limb uses 'may' and the second uses 'shall', so the duty arises when the evidence appears essential.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the 'shall'. Option B ignores the 'may'. Option C adds limits that the text does not contain.
questions.clat_trap: Students who recall only 'wide discretion' pick the first wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'May' versus 'shall' in the same provision is the language trick.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A High Court may, in an appropriate case, quash proceedings arising from a non-compoundable offence of a private character on the ground of settlement. Reason (R): Every non-compoundable offence becomes compoundable by the parties as of right once they settle.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is correct: such quashing is an exercise of inherent power on the strength of the settlement. R is false because compoundability is fixed by the statute for listed offences, and settlement-based quashing is a discretionary relief, not a right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Options A and B fail because R is false. Option D fails because A is true.
questions.clat_trap: R seems to explain A, since both speak of settlement. They rest on different legal bases, one discretionary and the other statutory.
questions.language_trick: 'As of right' is the words that make R false.

passages.title: Presumptions, Accomplices, Hostile Witnesses and Dying Declarations
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with effect from 1 July 2024, retains the main rules on presumptions and witnesses. Where the law says that the court 'may presume' a fact, the court has a discretion to regard the fact as proved unless it is disproved; where it says 'shall presume', the court must regard the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved; and where a fact is declared 'conclusive proof' of another, the court must regard the latter as proved and no evidence may be given to disprove it. An accomplice is a competent witness, and a conviction is not illegal merely because it rests on his uncorroborated testimony, but as a rule of prudence, courts seek corroboration in material particulars connecting the accused with the crime. A witness may be declared hostile with the leave of the court, and the party calling him may then cross-examine him. The Supreme Court has held that the evidence of a hostile witness is not completely effaced from the record, and the portions that are credible and corroborated may be relied upon by either side. A statement made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any circumstance of the transaction which resulted in his death, is relevant in a case where the cause of his death comes into question. It is admissible whether or not the maker was under expectation of death when he made it, which differs from the English rule. In Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002) a Constitution Bench held that a medical certificate of the declarant's fitness is not a requirement of law but a rule of caution, so that a dying declaration found by the court to be voluntary and truthful may be the sole basis of conviction. Where several dying declarations conflict, the court must scrutinise them with care. Under the provision on discovery, so much of the information received from an accused in police custody as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered is admissible, whether it amounts to a confession or not, and the rest is excluded.

questions.question: A is convicted solely on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice. On the passage the conviction is

options.A: not illegal in itself, though courts as a rule of prudence insist on corroboration in material particulars
options.B: legal only if the accomplice has been pardoned and has become an approver before the trial court
options.C: legal only if the trial judge records a finding that the accomplice is a man of good character and credit
options.D: illegal, because the law prohibits conviction on the sole evidence of an accomplice without independent support

questions.explanation: The passage separates legality from prudence: the conviction is not illegal, but courts seek corroboration.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns a rule of prudence into a rule of prohibition. Option C adds a condition about pardon. Option D adds a character test that does not exist.
questions.clat_trap: Practice has hardened the corroboration rule into near-law, so a student who knows the practice treats the conviction as illegal.
questions.language_trick: 'Not illegal merely because' separates law from prudence.

questions.question: A prosecution witness is declared hostile. He denies part of his earlier statement but supports the prosecution on another point, which is corroborated by a document. The court

options.A: must discard the entire testimony, because a hostile witness is wholly unreliable in law
options.B: may rely on the portion only if the court itself had summoned the witness
options.C: may rely on the corroborated portion, since his testimony is not wholly effaced
options.D: may rely on it only if the defence also consents

questions.explanation: A hostile witness's evidence is not completely effaced, and credible, corroborated portions may be relied upon by either side.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the old effaced-from-the-record view. Option B and Option D invent conditions.
questions.clat_trap: The label 'hostile' suggests total unreliability, and an absolute option is therefore tempting.
questions.language_trick: 'Not completely effaced' signals that a partial reliance is allowed.

questions.question: A dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate without a doctor's certificate of fitness is found by the court to be voluntary, consistent and truthful. On the passage

options.A: it is inadmissible, because a medical certificate of fitness is a requirement of law and cannot be dispensed with
options.B: it is admissible but must always be corroborated by independent evidence before any conviction can be founded on it
options.C: it is admissible only if the maker was expecting death at the time and had abandoned all hope of recovery
options.D: it can be the sole basis of conviction, since the certificate is a rule of caution

questions.explanation: Laxman holds that the certificate is a rule of caution, and a voluntary, truthful declaration can be the sole basis of conviction.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the position that Laxman rejected. Option B adds a corroboration requirement. Option C applies the English rule, which the passage says does not apply.
questions.clat_trap: The third wrong option is a rule that students know from English law.
questions.language_trick: 'Rule of caution' versus 'requirement of law' is the pair that decides the question.

questions.question: Z, believing he will die, names his attacker to a Magistrate but later recovers, and the attacker is tried for attempt to murder. On the passage the statement is

options.A: relevant as a dying declaration, since it concerns the circumstances of the transaction
options.B: not relevant as a dying declaration, since Z's death is not in question, though it may corroborate
options.C: relevant only if Z's expectation of death was recorded in writing by the attending doctor at the time of the statement
options.D: relevant as a dying declaration, since Z believed he would die

questions.explanation: The provision applies where the cause of the person's death comes into question. Z survived, so the dying-declaration route is closed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the requirement that death be in question, and expectation of death is not needed anyway. Option C also overlooks that requirement. Option D adds a medical record that is not required.
questions.clat_trap: The name 'dying declaration' and Z's belief in death distract from the actual condition that the maker's death must be in question.
questions.language_trick: 'Comes into question' and 'later recovers' decide the matter.

questions.question: The expression 'conclusive proof' differs from 'shall presume' in that

options.A: the former allows rebuttal, whereas the latter leaves the court a free choice
options.B: the former is permissive, while the latter requires the prosecution to prove the fact beyond reasonable doubt
options.C: both bar rebuttal, but only the former binds the court
options.D: evidence to disprove the fact is not allowed in the former but allowed in the latter

questions.explanation: Conclusive proof shuts out disproof. A shall-presume rule is rebuttable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the two. Option B makes both irrebuttable. Option C misdescribes both and brings in the criminal standard of proof.
questions.clat_trap: Three similar-sounding terms of art are easily confused, particularly under time pressure.
questions.language_trick: 'Shall' sounds absolute but only 'conclusive' bars rebuttal.

questions.question: An accused in police custody says: 'I killed X with an axe, which I hid in the cane field; I will show you.' The axe is recovered from the field. Under the passage the admissible portion is

options.A: only the part about where the axe was hidden, which led to its recovery
options.B: the whole statement, as the recovery of the axe proves it to be true
options.C: nothing at all, since a statement to a police officer is never admissible
options.D: the admission of the killing alone, since it is a confession in police custody

questions.explanation: Only the information relating distinctly to the fact discovered is admissible. The admission of the killing is excluded.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats recovery as validating the whole statement. Option C picks the inadmissible part. Option D uses 'never', which ignores the discovery provision.
questions.clat_trap: The recovery seems to prove the whole story, which tempts a student to admit all of it.
questions.language_trick: 'Relates distinctly' limits the admissible part.

passages.title: Res Judicata, Rejection of Plaint and the Limitation Act
passages.passage: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a court from trying a suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or parties litigating under the same title, and has been heard and finally decided by a competent court. Explanation IV treats as constructively in issue every matter which might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in the former suit. Order II Rule 2 separately requires a plaintiff to include the whole claim arising from a cause of action, failing which he cannot later sue for the portion omitted. Order VII Rule 11 empowers a court to reject a plaint where it discloses no cause of action, where the relief is undervalued or the stamp paper is insufficient and the plaintiff fails to correct it, or where the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by any law. The Supreme Court has held that, at this stage, the court examines only the plaint and the documents filed with it, taking the averments as true; the defence in the written statement is irrelevant, and a plaint cannot be rejected in part. Under the Limitation Act, 1963, Section 3 requires a court to dismiss a suit, appeal or application filed after the prescribed period, although limitation has not been set up as a defence. Section 5 allows an appeal or an application to be admitted after the period if the appellant shows sufficient cause, but it does not apply to suits. Section 14 excludes time spent prosecuting, with due diligence and in good faith, another civil proceeding in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, was unable to entertain it. Section 18 gives a fresh period of limitation where an acknowledgment of liability in writing, signed by the party, is made before the original period expires. Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, 1872 separately makes enforceable a written, signed promise to pay a debt barred by limitation.

questions.question: A sues B for a declaration of title to a plot on the basis of a sale deed, and the suit is dismissed on the merits after trial. A then files a fresh suit against B for the same plot, now pleading adverse possession, a ground that was open to him in the first suit. The second suit is

options.A: barred only if the earlier court expressly pronounced on adverse possession in its judgment
options.B: maintainable, since adverse possession is a different cause of action from a claim founded on a sale deed
options.C: barred, since adverse possession might and ought to have been raised as a ground of attack in the earlier suit
options.D: maintainable, since only issues actually framed and tried in the first suit can attract the bar of res judicata

questions.explanation: Explanation IV to Section 11 creates constructive res judicata: a ground which might and ought to have been taken is treated as if it had been taken and decided.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats a new legal ground as a new cause of action, which the Explanation does not allow. Option B limits the bar to issues actually tried, ignoring constructive res judicata. Option D requires an express finding, which is unnecessary for constructive bar.
questions.clat_trap: Students recall res judicata as 'what was actually decided' and miss the constructive limb. The factual detail that adverse possession was 'open' in the first suit is the cue.
questions.language_trick: 'might and ought to have been' is a double test: availability and obligation to plead.

questions.question: In a suit for recovery, the defendant applies under Order VII Rule 11 to reject the plaint as time-barred, relying on documents he has annexed to his written statement. The plaint, read alone, shows the suit to be within time. The application should be

options.A: allowed, since the defendant's undisputed documents annexed to his written statement may always be considered to test whether the plaint is time-barred
options.B: kept pending until a full trial on limitation, after which the plaint can be rejected at the end
options.C: allowed in part, by rejecting only the relief that appears time-barred and leaving the remainder
options.D: dismissed, since only the plaint and the documents filed with it are examined, its averments taken as true

questions.explanation: At the Order VII Rule 11 stage the defence is irrelevant. A plaint cannot be rejected in part, and a triable question of limitation requires a trial.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A brings in the defence, which the passage excludes. Option B contradicts the rule that a plaint cannot be rejected in part. Option C treats rejection as a post-trial remedy, though it is a threshold power.
questions.clat_trap: The applicant's documents look reliable, so a student is tempted to consider them. The Order VII Rule 11 filter is only the plaint.
questions.language_trick: 'taking the averments as true' fixes the court's vantage point.

questions.question: A plaintiff files a suit twenty days after the period of limitation has expired, together with an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act showing sufficient cause for the delay. The court should

options.A: condone the delay only if the defendant raises no objection to the application made by the plaintiff on this ground
options.B: dismiss the suit as time-barred, since Section 5 is confined to appeals and applications
options.C: admit the suit and decide limitation after evidence has been led, as it is a mixed question of fact and law
options.D: condone the delay if the cause shown is sufficient, as Section 5 covers all proceedings including the institution of suits

questions.explanation: Section 5 does not extend to suits. A suit filed late is dismissed under Section 3 unless an exclusion such as Section 12 or 14 applies.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A extends Section 5 to suits. Option C makes condonation depend on the defendant's consent, which is not the test. Option D turns a plain statutory bar into a trial issue.
questions.clat_trap: The phrase 'sufficient cause' is familiar, so the student assumes it works everywhere.
questions.language_trick: 'suit' versus 'appeal or application': the entire question turns on one noun.

questions.question: A debt became barred by limitation on 1 January 2023. On 1 March 2023 the debtor writes to the creditor, signing the letter, and promises to pay the whole amount in instalments. Which statement is correct?

options.A: the debt stays extinguished for every purpose, as no promise can ever revive a time-barred debt, however it is made or signed by the debtor
options.B: the promise is enforceable only if the creditor gave fresh consideration at the time of the letter, whatever its terms or form
options.C: Section 18 gives a fresh period of three years from 1 March 2023, since an acknowledgment revives the right to sue on the debt in every case, whatever the date of the letter
options.D: Section 18 gives no fresh period, as the acknowledgment came after expiry, but the signed promise may be enforceable under Section 25(3)

questions.explanation: Section 18 requires the acknowledgment to be made before the original period expires. A later signed written promise to pay a barred debt is separately enforceable under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the word 'before' in Section 18. Option B overlooks Section 25(3). Option C asks for consideration, which Section 25(3) dispenses with.
questions.clat_trap: Two statutes, one set of facts. Students apply only one, and the date of the letter after expiry is the hidden cue.
questions.language_trick: 'before the original period expires' is the temporal condition on which everything depends.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A plaintiff whose earlier suit failed for want of jurisdiction can always claim exclusion of the whole time spent in that suit when suing afresh on the same matter. Reason (R): Section 14 of the Limitation Act excludes time spent in a civil proceeding in a court which was unable to entertain it for defect of jurisdiction.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Section 14 is conditional, not automatic. The earlier proceeding must have been prosecuted with due diligence and in good faith. R is a correct statement of the provision, but A overstates it by using 'always'.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is false because of the word 'always', while R accurately paraphrases the provision.
questions.clat_trap: A student who agrees with the thrust of Section 14 marks A as true. The absolute word is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'always' removes the conditions of good faith and due diligence.

questions.question: The defendant does not plead limitation in his written statement, and the suit is plainly filed after the prescribed period. The court

options.A: may decree the suit but must reduce the relief in proportion to the delay
options.B: may proceed to decree, since limitation is a personal defence which the defendant's silence waives completely
options.C: must dismiss the suit, as Section 3 operates even when limitation is not set up as a defence
options.D: must frame an issue on limitation only if the defendant asks for it at the final hearing

questions.explanation: Section 3 expressly requires dismissal although limitation has not been set up as a defence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats limitation as a waivable personal plea. Option B makes the court's duty depend on a request. Option D invents a proportionate-relief rule.
questions.clat_trap: Ordinary defences are waived if not pleaded, so students extend that rule to limitation.
questions.language_trick: 'although ... has not been set up' signals that the court's duty is independent of pleading.

passages.subject_area: Law of Contract and Government Contracts
passages.title: Void Agreements, Promissory Estoppel, Article 299 and Section 70
passages.passage: Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 makes agreements contracts if made by free consent of competent parties for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and not expressly declared void. Section 27 declares void every agreement by which a person is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business. Courts have held that a covenant restraining an employee during the term of employment is not a restraint of trade, because it protects the employer's legitimate interest while the service lasts, whereas a post-termination restraint is void. Section 28 declares void an agreement that restricts a party from enforcing his rights by ordinary legal proceedings, but saves arbitration agreements, and the Court has held that parties may choose between courts that already have jurisdiction, though they cannot by agreement confer jurisdiction on a court that has none. The doctrine of promissory estoppel prevents a promisor from going back on a clear promise intended to create legal relations, on which the promisee has relied by altering his position. In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of U.P., the Supreme Court held that the doctrine can be invoked against the Government and can found a cause of action; it will not, however, be enforced where the public interest outweighs the equity, nor can it compel the Government to act contrary to law or its legislative power. Article 299(1) of the Constitution requires that contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or a State be expressed to be made by the President or the Governor and be executed by persons authorised on his behalf. The Court has treated these requirements as mandatory, so that a non-compliant contract does not bind the Government. Section 70 of the Contract Act, however, provides that where a person lawfully does something for another, not intending to do so gratuitously, and the other enjoys the benefit, the latter must compensate the former. The Court has held that Section 70 may apply to the Government even though the Article 299 formalities were not met, since the claim rests on restitution and not on contract.

questions.question: An employment contract bars a software engineer from working for any rival firm for the three years during which he remains in service. He moonlights for a rival, and the employer seeks an injunction. On the passage, the clause is

options.A: enforceable only if a reasonable post-service period is also stipulated in the contract
options.B: void under Section 28, since it restricts him from enforcing his rights through legal proceedings
options.C: enforceable, being a restraint that operates only during employment and not a restraint of trade under Section 27
options.D: void under Section 27, since it prevents him from earning a livelihood through his profession

questions.explanation: Covenants operating during employment are not treated as restraint of trade. Section 27 bites on post-termination restraints.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies Section 27 without the employment distinction. Option B confuses Section 28, which concerns legal proceedings. Option D adds a condition that has no basis.
questions.clat_trap: Section 27 is widely remembered as 'all restraints are void', so students overlook the in-service exception.
questions.language_trick: 'during the term of employment' marks the exception.

questions.question: A contractor builds a road for a State on a letter from an Executive Engineer. No contract in the form required by Article 299 exists, and the State has put the road to use. The contractor's best remedy is

options.A: promissory estoppel, to compel payment at the full rate named in the letter
options.B: enforcement of the letter as a contract, because Article 299 is merely directory and the State has benefited
options.C: none, since a contract void under Article 299 cannot give rise to any liability at all
options.D: compensation under Section 70 for the benefit the State has enjoyed, not enforcement of the informal contract

questions.explanation: The Article 299 formalities are mandatory, so the contract cannot be enforced. Section 70 allows restitution for the benefit enjoyed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the mandatory nature of Article 299. Option B uses estoppel to enforce a contract the Constitution makes non-binding. Option C ignores Section 70.
questions.clat_trap: The choice is between three tempting remedies. The only one consistent with both Article 299 and the quasi-contract rule is restitution.
questions.language_trick: 'not on contract but restitution' distinguishes the measure of recovery.

questions.question: Which statement about promissory estoppel against the Government is accurate on the passage?

options.A: It binds the Government absolutely, even where fulfilling the promise would contravene a statute
options.B: It can found a cause of action but yields where the public interest outweighs the equity
options.C: It arises only if the promisee proves a measurable financial loss from relying on the promise
options.D: It operates only as a shield and can never found an action against the Government

questions.explanation: Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills allowed the doctrine to ground a cause of action while recognising the public-interest limit.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the narrower English position, which the Court did not adopt. Option C ignores the limit based on law and legislative power. Option D adds a loss requirement.
questions.clat_trap: Three options are half-truths drawn from different jurisdictions and doctrines.
questions.language_trick: 'absolutely' and 'can never' are overstatements.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Once a State promises a tax holiday to a new industrial unit and the unit invests in reliance, the State can never withdraw the exemption. Reason (R): Promissory estoppel can be invoked against the Government.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is correct per Motilal. A is wrong because the doctrine does not apply where the public interest outweighs the equity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is false because of 'never'; R is a true proposition.
questions.clat_trap: A true-sounding R tempts students to accept A as its consequence.
questions.language_trick: 'never' removes the public-interest exception.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT required for a claim under Section 70 of the Contract Act?

options.A: That the act was not done with the intention of acting gratuitously, that is, free of charge
options.B: A subsisting contract between the claimant and the recipient
options.C: That the act was done lawfully for the other person and not in some unlawful enterprise
options.D: That the other person enjoyed the benefit of the act, and not merely received an offer of it

questions.explanation: Section 70 is a quasi-contractual remedy that operates where there is no contract. The other three are its ingredients.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D are all ingredients of the section.
questions.clat_trap: In a 'NOT' stem, the three familiar elements are placed as decoys.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT required' reverses the usual selection logic.

questions.question: A contract provides that all disputes shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts at Delhi. The cause of action arises wholly in Mumbai, where the defendant also resides; Delhi courts have no connection with the dispute. On the passage,

options.A: Delhi courts can hear the suit, but only if the defendant consents after the dispute has arisen
options.B: Delhi courts can hear the suit, as parties may freely choose any forum whatever under the saving in Section 28
options.C: Delhi courts cannot hear it, as parties cannot by agreement confer jurisdiction on a court that has none
options.D: the whole clause is void as an ouster of all courts, and the contract itself fails with it

questions.explanation: Parties may select between courts that already have jurisdiction, but cannot create jurisdiction by agreement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads Section 28's saving too widely. Option B adds a consent rule that does not exist. Option D confuses a forum clause with an ouster of all courts.
questions.clat_trap: Exclusive-jurisdiction clauses are usually upheld, so students assume the clause always works.
questions.language_trick: 'already have jurisdiction' limits the choice to existing competent courts.

passages.title: Dishonour of Cheques under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act
passages.passage: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes it an offence, punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both, where a cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him is returned unpaid because of insufficient funds or because it exceeds the arrangement with the bank. The cheque must have been issued in discharge, wholly or partly, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability, and presented within the period of its validity, which is three months from its date. The payee must give written notice demanding payment within thirty days of receiving information from the bank of the dishonour, and the offence is complete only if the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receiving the notice. A complaint must be filed within one month of the date on which that cause of action arises, though the court may take cognisance after delay on sufficient cause. Sections 118(a) and 139 raise presumptions that the instrument was made for consideration and that the holder received it in discharge of a legally enforceable debt. The Supreme Court has held that these presumptions are rebuttable and that the accused need only raise a probable defence, by the standard of preponderance of probabilities, and need not enter the witness box. Under Section 141, where a company commits the offence, every person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of its business at the time is liable; a mere directorship is not enough, though the signatory of the cheque is liable. After the 2015 amendment, Section 142(2) places jurisdiction, in the case of a cheque delivered for collection through an account, in the court within whose local limits the branch of the bank where the payee maintains the account is situated. Section 143A permits interim compensation of up to twenty per cent of the cheque amount.

questions.question: A cheque issued to settle a gambling debt is dishonoured for insufficient funds, and the payee follows every statutory step. On the passage, the drawer

options.A: is liable only if the payee did not know the debt was unenforceable when accepting the cheque
options.B: is liable, because the presumption under Section 139 is conclusive once the cheque is dishonoured
options.C: is liable, because the statute is concerned only with dishonour and not with the underlying transaction
options.D: is not liable under Section 138, since the cheque was not issued for a legally enforceable debt

questions.explanation: The cheque must be issued for a legally enforceable debt or liability. A gambling debt is not one, and the presumption is rebuttable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats a rebuttable presumption as conclusive. Option B ignores the first ingredient of the offence. Option C imports the payee's knowledge, which is irrelevant.
questions.clat_trap: Dishonour looks like the whole offence, but the existence of a legally enforceable debt is an ingredient.
questions.language_trick: 'legally enforceable' is the operative phrase.

questions.question: The bank informs the payee on 1 March that the cheque has been dishonoured. The payee sends the demand notice on 5 April. The drawer does not pay, and the payee files a complaint within a month of the fifteen days expiring. On the passage,

options.A: the complaint succeeds, since the thirty days run from the date of the cheque and not from the bank's information
options.B: the complaint succeeds, since the court can condone delay in sending the notice if the payee shows sufficient cause
options.C: the complaint succeeds, since the notice was sent within the month allowed for filing the complaint after the cause arose
options.D: the complaint fails, since the notice was sent more than thirty days after the payee received the bank's information

questions.explanation: The notice must be given within thirty days of information of dishonour. Condonation applies to the complaint, not to the notice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A mixes the complaint period with the notice period. Option B uses the wrong starting date. Option C extends the condonation power beyond the complaint.
questions.clat_trap: Two different time limits are used. The student must apply the right one to the right step.
questions.language_trick: 'within thirty days of receiving information' fixes the clock.

questions.question: On the presumption under Section 139, the accused in a Section 138 prosecution

options.A: must prove beyond reasonable doubt that no debt existed
options.B: may rebut it by raising a probable defence on a preponderance of probabilities, even without leading his own evidence
options.C: may rebut it only by stepping into the witness box and testifying
options.D: need not rebut it at all once the cheque is shown to bear his signature, as it is conclusive

questions.explanation: The presumption is rebuttable. The standard is preponderance of probabilities and the accused can rely on material in the complainant's case.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the criminal standard to the accused. Option C makes testimony mandatory. Option D treats the presumption as irrebuttable.
questions.clat_trap: The accused's burden is often misread as the prosecution's standard.
questions.language_trick: 'probable defence' signals a lower threshold.

questions.question: A complaint against a non-executive director of a company names him as 'director' only, with no averment that he was in charge of or responsible for its business, and he did not sign the cheque. The best view is that

options.A: the complaint against him should be quashed, as mere directorship does not attract Section 141 without such an averment
options.B: the complaint is bad only if the company itself is not joined as an accused
options.C: the complaint stands, since lack of knowledge can be proved only at trial and never at the quashing stage
options.D: the complaint stands, since directors are always vicariously liable for the company's cheques

questions.explanation: Section 141 requires that the person was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business. The complaint must say so.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B equates directorship with liability. Option C uses an absolute rule on quashing. Option D confuses the need to join the company with the need to plead the director's role.
questions.clat_trap: 'Director' sounds like 'responsible'. The distinction between status and role is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'mere directorship' is a signal phrase.

questions.question: A payee in Pune deposits a cheque drawn on a Chennai bank into his own account at a Pune branch, and the cheque is dishonoured. Where may he file the complaint?

options.A: Only at Chennai, where the drawer's bank branch is located, since the dishonour occurred at that branch
options.B: In any court in India, since the offence is a continuing one
options.C: In the court at Pune, where the payee's account branch is situated, under amended Section 142(2)
options.D: Only where the drawer resides or carries on business, since the offence lies in non-payment

questions.explanation: After the 2015 amendment, jurisdiction lies at the place of the payee's account branch where the cheque is delivered for collection through an account.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the position before the 2015 amendment. Option B picks a different anchor. Option D ignores territorial limits.
questions.clat_trap: Earlier case law pointed to the drawer's bank, so the old rule is a ready distractor.
questions.language_trick: 'delivered for collection through an account' defines when the rule applies.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A drawer who pays the cheque amount within fifteen days of receiving the demand notice cannot be convicted under Section 138. Reason (R): The offence is complete only if the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of receiving the notice.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Dishonour alone is not the offence. Non-payment within the notice period completes it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states the element whose absence makes A true.
questions.clat_trap: Students assume the offence is complete at dishonour.
questions.language_trick: 'only if' makes the failure an essential element.

passages.title: Negligence: Remoteness, Res Ipsa Loquitur and Professional Liability
passages.passage: Liability in negligence requires a duty of care, a breach of that duty by falling below the standard of a reasonable person, and damage caused by the breach which is not too remote. Following The Wagon Mound (No. 1), a defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable, but if damage of that kind is foreseeable he takes the victim as he finds him, so that he is liable for its full extent even where an unusually fragile claimant suffers more than a normal person would (the eggshell skull rule). The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applies where the thing causing the harm was under the defendant's control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence; it permits the court to infer negligence, and calls for an explanation from the defendant, but does not by itself shift the legal burden of proof. Contributory negligence is a partial defence: damages are apportioned according to the claimant's share of fault, and the claimant's omission must have contributed to his own harm. In medical negligence, Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab held that a professional is judged by the standard of an ordinary competent practitioner exercising the skill he professes, and that criminal liability requires gross negligence or recklessness, not mere lack of care. Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 prescribes a lower maximum term of imprisonment for a registered medical practitioner whose rash or negligent act causes death. An employer is ordinarily not liable for the torts of an independent contractor, but is liable where the duty owed to the claimant is non-delegable, as where a hospital holds out a doctor as part of its own service and the patient relies on it.

questions.question: A negligently spills oil on a harbour. Fire breaks out because welding sparks ignite floating cotton waste on the oil, a kind of damage no reasonable person in A's position could have foreseen. Beyond the fouling of the harbour, A is

options.A: liable for the fire, but only for half the loss, as the welder shared the fault
options.B: not liable for the fire, since that kind of damage was not reasonably foreseeable
options.C: liable for the fire, since it flowed directly from the spill whether or not foreseeable
options.D: liable for the fire, since he must take the harbour as he finds it

questions.explanation: Under The Wagon Mound, liability extends only to damage of a kind that is reasonably foreseeable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the discarded directness test. Option C misuses the eggshell skull rule, which concerns the extent of foreseeable harm. Option D invents an apportionment.
questions.clat_trap: Directness tempts the student, because the fire does follow from the spill.
questions.language_trick: 'a kind of damage' is the unit of the foreseeability test.

questions.question: A drives negligently and lightly taps B's car. B, who has an unusually thin skull, suffers a severe fracture that a normal person would not. Some physical injury was foreseeable. A is

options.A: liable for the full extent of B's injury, as he takes his victim as he finds him
options.B: liable for the full injury only if A knew of B's condition before the collision
options.C: not liable, since B's thin skull was an intervening act which broke the chain of causation
options.D: liable only for the minor injury a normal person would have suffered, since the fracture's extent was unforeseeable

questions.explanation: The eggshell skull rule makes the defendant liable for the full extent of a foreseeable kind of damage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B confuses kind of damage with its extent. Option C treats a pre-existing condition as an intervening act. Option D adds a knowledge requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The Wagon Mound's foreseeability test is mistakenly applied to extent.
questions.language_trick: 'kind' versus 'extent'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Where res ipsa loquitur applies, the defendant must always disprove negligence, failing which the claimant must succeed. Reason (R): The doctrine permits the court to infer negligence where the thing was under the defendant's control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is accurate. A is wrong because the doctrine raises an inference and calls for an explanation, but does not by itself shift the legal burden.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is false, R is true.
questions.clat_trap: Many textbooks loosely say the burden shifts. The passage is more precise.
questions.language_trick: 'always disprove' overstates the effect.

questions.question: A registered medical practitioner's patient dies after a lapse of ordinary care that falls short of gross negligence. On the passage, which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Both civil and criminal liability arise, as any lapse of care causing death attracts the Sanhita
options.B: Civil liability in compensation may arise, but criminal liability needs gross negligence or recklessness
options.C: Criminal liability arises, but only the lower maximum term applies under Section 106(1)
options.D: Neither arises, since the practitioner is judged by the highest skill available in the profession
