questions.explanation: The civil standard is the ordinary competent practitioner. The criminal threshold is higher.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A equates civil and criminal thresholds. Option C states a standard the passage rejects. Option D assumes criminal liability exists and only debates the penalty.
questions.clat_trap: The sentencing provision in the passage tempts the student to presume the offence is made out.
questions.language_trick: 'ordinary' versus 'gross'.

questions.question: A motorcyclist riding without a helmet is hit by a negligent car driver and suffers a head injury that a helmet would have prevented, although the collision itself was wholly the driver's fault. The best view is that

options.A: the claim fails completely, since contributory negligence is a complete defence to the action
options.B: damages are reduced by half, since the claimant's fault is presumed equal to the defendant's
options.C: damages are reduced to the extent that the missing helmet contributed to the harm
options.D: damages remain undiminished, since the omission did not cause the collision

questions.explanation: Contributory negligence asks whether the claimant's omission contributed to his own harm, not to the accident.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats the defence as complete. Option B confuses the cause of the accident with the cause of the injury. Option D invents a presumption.
questions.clat_trap: 'Did not cause the collision' feels decisive, but the passage focuses on harm.
questions.language_trick: 'his own harm' is the key phrase.

questions.question: A private hospital advertises its surgeons as 'our team'. A visiting consultant, an independent practitioner paid per procedure, performs a negligent surgery on a patient. The hospital says it is not liable for an independent contractor. On the passage,

options.A: the hospital may be liable, since it held the consultant out as part of its own service and the duty was non-delegable
options.B: liable only if the consultant is on its payroll as a regular employee at the time of the operation on the patient
options.C: liable, but only for damages equal to the fee it received from the patient and not for any wider loss of the patient
options.D: not liable, since an employer is never answerable for the negligence of an independent contractor engaged by it for any work

questions.explanation: An employer is liable for an independent contractor where the duty is non-delegable, as where the hospital holds out the doctor as part of its service.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the general rule without the exception. Option C limits liability to employees. Option D invents a cap.
questions.clat_trap: The general rule is stated first and the exception is the heart of the question.
questions.language_trick: 'holds out' is the trigger for the exception.

passages.title: Gifts, Transfers to Unborn Persons and the Rule against Perpetuities
passages.passage: Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines gift as the transfer of existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration by one person, the donor, to another, the donee, and accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Acceptance must be made during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving; if the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void. Section 123 requires that a gift of immovable property be effected by a registered instrument signed by the donor and attested by at least two witnesses, whereas a gift of movable property may be effected either by such an instrument or by delivery. The Supreme Court has held that delivery of possession is not essential to the validity of a gift of immovable property made by such a registered instrument. Section 124 declares a gift comprising both existing and future property void as to the latter. Section 126 provides that a gift which the parties agree shall be revocable wholly or in part at the mere will of the donor is void wholly or in part, though parties may validly agree that it shall be revocable on a specified event not depending on the donor's will. Section 13 provides that where property is transferred for the benefit of an unborn person, no interest is created for his benefit unless it is preceded by an interest in favour of a person in existence at the date of the transfer, and the interest created for the unborn person extends to the whole of the remaining interest of the transferor. Section 14 enacts the rule against perpetuities: no transfer of property can operate to create an interest which is to take effect after the lifetime of one or more persons living at the date of the transfer, and the minority of some person who shall be in existence at the expiration of that period, and to whom, if he attains full age, the interest created is to belong. A transfer for the benefit of the public in the advancement of religion, knowledge, commerce, health or safety is excepted.

questions.question: A donor orally declares in the presence of friends a gift of his house to his nephew, and hands over the keys and possession. No deed is executed. On the passage, the gift is

options.A: valid, but only if the two friends later swear to the declaration before a court
options.B: valid, since the nephew accepted it and no consideration was paid
options.C: valid, since delivery of possession alone completes a gift of immovable property
options.D: invalid, since a gift of immovable property requires a registered instrument attested by two witnesses

questions.explanation: Section 123 requires a registered and attested instrument for gift of immovable property.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats delivery as enough, which applies only to movables. Option B stresses acceptance and absence of consideration but ignores form. Option C invents a court-affirmation route.
questions.clat_trap: Delivery of possession is the familiar sign of a completed transfer, but not for immovables.
questions.language_trick: 'immovable' versus 'movable' decides the mode.

questions.question: A executes a deed gifting to B his house and also 'whatever property I may inherit from my father'. A's father later dies, leaving A a farm. The gift is

options.A: valid as to both, since the farm vested in A before B claimed it
options.B: void as to the house too, since the gift of future property taints the whole instrument
options.C: valid as to the farm if A later confirms the gift by a registered deed within three years
options.D: void as to the farm, being future property, though valid as to the house

questions.explanation: Section 124 voids a gift only as to future property. The gift of the house stands.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the word 'existing' in Section 122. Option B extends the invalidity beyond the future property. Option C invents a confirmation period.
questions.clat_trap: A single deed combining valid and invalid parts tempts students to treat it as all or nothing.
questions.language_trick: 'void as to the latter' limits the invalidity.

questions.question: A deed gifts land to B 'absolutely, but revocable by A at any time at his sole pleasure'. B accepts. A later purports to revoke. On the passage,

options.A: valid for B's lifetime but reverts to A's heirs on his death, as the donor's reservation limits the interest
options.B: valid, with only the revocation clause struck off as void, and B takes an absolute interest free of any condition
options.C: void, since a gift revocable wholly at the mere will of the donor is not a valid gift
options.D: valid, and A's revocation is effective since he expressly reserved the right to revoke it at his sole pleasure

questions.explanation: Section 126 declares a gift revocable at the mere will of the donor void to that extent. Where the whole gift is so revocable, it is void altogether.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A severs the clause, which would keep the gift alive. Option B enforces a reservation that the Act declares void. Option D invents a reversion.
questions.clat_trap: Severing the clause looks like the neat solution, and it is the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'wholly or in part, as the case may be' is the language to read closely.

questions.question: A transfers land to B for life, then to B's unborn son C for C's life, and after C's death to D absolutely. B is alive and C is not yet born. Which is correct?

options.A: C's interest is valid, since B, a person in existence, holds the prior interest
options.B: every interest fails, including B's, since a gift to an unborn person taints the whole transfer
options.C: B's interest stands, but C's fails, as it is not A's whole remaining interest
options.D: C's interest is valid and D's is void, as the rule against perpetuities cuts off the last interest

questions.explanation: Section 13 needs both a prior interest in a living person and a transfer of the whole remaining interest to the unborn person. C is given only a life interest.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overextends the invalidity to B. Option B satisfies the first condition but ignores the second. Option D wrongly applies Section 14 to the last remainder.
questions.clat_trap: A student checks the prior-interest condition and stops, forgetting the second.
questions.language_trick: 'whole of the remaining interest' is the second condition.

questions.question: A transfers land to B for life, and then to B's unborn child C 'who shall take the land on attaining twenty-five'. C is born later. The interest in C is

options.A: void, since it may vest after the lifetime of B and the minority of C, which is beyond the permitted period
options.B: valid for the first twenty-five years and void thereafter, as courts cut down excessive periods to the limit
options.C: valid, since the age of vesting is the transferor's choice and the rule only restricts indefinite vesting
options.D: valid, since B, a person in existence, holds the prior life interest and C takes the whole remainder

questions.explanation: Section 14 permits vesting within the life of a person in being plus the minority of the person to whom the interest belongs. Vesting at twenty-five can exceed that period.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B satisfies Section 13 but ignores Section 14. Option C misreads the rule. Option D assumes a cy-près power that the Act does not give.
questions.clat_trap: Section 13 is satisfied, so the student stops. A second statute is hidden in the age of vesting.
questions.language_trick: 'minority' means until the age of full age (eighteen), not the age chosen by the transferor.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A gift fails if the donee dies before accepting it. Reason (R): Acceptance is an essential element of a gift and must take place during the donor's lifetime while he is capable of giving.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Section 122 requires acceptance during the donor's lifetime and provides that the gift is void if the donee dies before acceptance.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states the requirement from which A follows.
questions.clat_trap: Students who treat the gift as complete on execution overlook acceptance.
questions.language_trick: 'before accepting' links directly to the condition in R.

passages.title: The Hindu Marriage Act: Validity, Voidability and Dissolution
passages.passage: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 prescribes conditions for a valid marriage in Section 5: neither party may have a spouse living at the time of marriage; neither may be incapable of giving valid consent through unsoundness of mind, or be so affected by mental disorder as to be unfit for marriage and procreation; the bridegroom must have completed twenty-one years and the bride eighteen; and the parties must not be within the degrees of prohibited relationship or sapindas of each other, unless custom permits. Section 11 declares a marriage void if it contravenes the conditions of monogamy, prohibited relationship or sapinda relationship, and a petition may be presented by either party. Section 12 makes a marriage voidable on grounds such as impotence at the time of marriage and its continuance until the institution of proceedings, unsoundness of mind, consent obtained by force or fraud as to the nature of the ceremony or a material circumstance, or pregnancy of the wife by some person other than the husband at the time of marriage. A voidable marriage is valid until annulled. Breach of the age condition does not make the marriage void or voidable, though it is punishable. Section 16 treats children of a void or voidable marriage as legitimate, but confines their rights to the property of their parents. Section 9 permits a spouse to seek restitution of conjugal rights where the other has withdrawn from society without reasonable excuse. Section 13 lists the grounds of divorce, including adultery, cruelty and desertion for two years, while Section 13B permits divorce by mutual consent after a year of separation, the six-month waiting period being treated as directory and waivable by a court in appropriate cases. In Shilpa Sailesh (2023), a Constitution Bench held that the Supreme Court may dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown in exercise of its power under Article 142, though breakdown is not a statutory ground for divorce.

questions.question: A marries B while his first wife is alive and no custom permits a second marriage. In law this marriage is

options.A: valid until annulled by a court on a petition by B, being a voidable marriage
options.B: valid, but punishable and no more than that, as the marriage itself stands
options.C: voidable at the option of the first wife alone, who must petition within a limited period
options.D: void, and either party may seek a declaration of nullity

questions.explanation: Section 5(i) read with Section 11 makes the marriage void from the start, and a petition can be presented by either party.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B treat it as voidable, which would need a decree to end it. Option C confuses bigamy with the age-condition breach.
questions.clat_trap: Voidable and void are interchanged in options, and the first wife is wrongly given the sole right.
questions.language_trick: 'either party' in Section 11 is wide, and the stem does not restrict the petitioner.

questions.question: A bride aged seventeen is married to a groom aged twenty-two with proper rites. The marriage under the Act is

options.A: void ab initio, since Section 5 sets the minimum age as a condition of every Hindu marriage and it was not met
options.B: valid, since breach of the age condition is punishable but does not itself invalidate it
options.C: voidable at the option of the bride on attaining majority, as with a marriage solemnised without her free consent
options.D: void unless the parents of the bride gave written consent to the marriage before the rites were performed

questions.explanation: Neither Section 11 nor Section 12 lists the age condition, so the marriage remains valid though the offence is punishable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A assumes every condition in Section 5 leads to nullity. Option C imports a ground from other laws. Option D adds a parental-consent rule that the Act no longer has.
questions.clat_trap: A student sees Section 5 as a list of conditions all of which lead to nullity.
questions.language_trick: 'punishable' is not 'void'.

questions.question: A husband seeks annulment on the ground that his wife was pregnant by another person when they married. Which condition is NOT part of this ground as the passage frames it?

options.A: That the husband had no sexual relations with her after discovering the pregnancy
options.B: That the petitioner was ignorant of the fact at the time of the marriage
options.C: That the pregnancy existed at the time of the marriage and was of a person other than the husband
options.D: That the person was not the husband

questions.explanation: The ground needs pregnancy at the time of marriage by another person. Post-discovery conduct is not an element in the passage, although it may matter for relief.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B and Option D are elements of the ground in the passage. Option C is a standard condition read from the Act, in that the petitioner must have been unaware.
questions.clat_trap: The stem asks which is NOT a part, and three of four options look natural.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT part of this ground': a negative stem.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A child born of a voidable marriage that is annulled is legitimate and may inherit the self-acquired property of the parents' relatives. Reason (R): Section 16 confines the rights of such children to the property of their parents.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because Section 16 gives rights only in the parents' property, not that of relatives. R is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The first half of A is correct, while the second half breaches the limitation in R.
questions.clat_trap: A starts with a correct proposition, and the trap is in the last clause.
questions.language_trick: 'relatives' vs 'parents': one word changes the answer.

questions.question: Spouse X files a petition for restitution of conjugal rights. The respondent answers that she left because X habitually abused her. On the passage, the likely result is

options.A: the petition succeeds, since cruelty is a ground only for divorce
options.B: the petition succeeds, since the respondent has not sought divorce
options.C: the petition fails since the withdrawal was with reasonable excuse
options.D: the petition is dismissed only if the respondent first proves adultery

questions.explanation: Section 9 requires withdrawal without reasonable excuse. Abuse is a reasonable excuse.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A suggests excuses must meet a divorce ground. Option B makes a counterclaim a condition of defence. Option D imports an unrelated requirement.
questions.clat_trap: A student reads the grounds in Section 13 as the only excuses that count under Section 9.
questions.language_trick: 'reasonable excuse' is broader than any statutory ground.

questions.question: Irretrievable breakdown is described in the passage as

options.A: a ground added to Section 13 by the Constitution Bench in Shilpa Sailesh, which now applies as a statutory ground
options.B: a ground the Supreme Court may act on under Article 142, not one in the statute
options.C: a ground that every Family Court may apply after one year of separation between the spouses without any special power
options.D: a ground that the Court may use only with the consent of both spouses to the dissolution of the marriage

questions.explanation: The Court used Article 142 and did not amend the Act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A claims a judicial amendment of the statute. Option C extends the power to Family Courts. Option D adds a consent requirement, which would make it identical to Section 13B.
questions.clat_trap: A student assumes judicial recognition equals statutory recognition.
questions.language_trick: 'though breakdown is not a statutory ground' limits the holding.

passages.title: Jurisdiction, Immunity and Extradition
passages.passage: Public international law allows a State to exercise jurisdiction on several bases: territory, nationality, the protective principle and, for certain crimes such as piracy and genocide, universality. In the Lotus case (1927), the Permanent Court of International Justice said that a State may exercise jurisdiction unless a prohibitive rule restrains it, a view since modified by the requirement of a genuine link. Immunity limits jurisdiction. Under the restrictive theory, a foreign State is immune for sovereign acts (acta jure imperii) but not for commercial or private acts (acta jure gestionis). In Jurisdictional Immunities of the State (Germany v. Italy, 2012), the International Court of Justice held that State immunity applied to acts of armed forces in armed conflict even when serious violations of international law were alleged. Personal immunity attaches to certain officials while in office: in the Arrest Warrant case (2002), the Court held that an incumbent foreign minister enjoyed immunity from the criminal jurisdiction of another State, though not before national courts of his own State or after leaving office for private acts. The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961 grants a diplomatic agent immunity from criminal jurisdiction, while immunity from civil jurisdiction is subject to exceptions, such as private immovable property and actions in a professional capacity outside official functions. Immunity belongs to the sending State and can be waived only by it, expressly. In India, Section 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 bars suits against foreign States without the consent of the Central Government. Extradition is governed by treaties and, in India, by the Extradition Act, 1962. Its principles include double criminality, specialty (the requesting State may try the person only for the offence for which extradition was granted) and the political offence exception. In Abu Salem (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Union was bound by its assurance to Portugal under the principle of specialty and could not detain beyond the agreed period.

questions.question: A foreign State enters into a contract with an Indian firm for the commercial supply of grain, and later defaults. Under the restrictive theory in the passage, the foreign State

options.A: not immune, and the Central Government's consent under Section 86 is not needed at all in any suit against it
options.B: not immune, as it acted commercially, though Section 86 still governs the suit
options.C: immune, because the contract was signed on behalf of its government and by a person holding public office in that State
options.D: immune, because every act of a sovereign State is public in nature and no commercial purpose can alter that character

questions.explanation: The act is jure gestionis. The passage still says that Section 86 CPC bars suits without the Central Government's consent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option C reflect the absolute theory. Option D ignores the procedural bar in Section 86.
questions.clat_trap: The right answer has two parts, one substantive (no immunity) and one procedural (consent), and the last wrong option drops the second part.
questions.language_trick: 'though Section 86 still governs' is the nuance.

questions.question: A former foreign minister is sought to be prosecuted by a State for a private act done after he left office. On the passage, immunity

options.A: does not bar prosecution for private post-office acts
options.B: lasts for one year after leaving office, after which the immunity ends
options.C: continues until the sending State consents to the prosecution of its former minister
options.D: continues for life, since a minister once immune is always immune from foreign courts

questions.explanation: The Arrest Warrant case limited the immunity to incumbent officials in respect of private acts.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B gives lifetime immunity. Option C imports a waiver requirement for former officials. Option D invents a cooling-off period.
questions.clat_trap: A student applies the wide immunity of an incumbent to a former official.
questions.language_trick: 'former' and 'private acts' take the case outside the rule.

questions.question: Which statement about the Jurisdictional Immunities case (2012) is correct as described?

options.A: The Court recognised immunity for armed forces' acts in conflict despite allegations of grave violations
options.B: The Court held that Italy's courts could try the claims, since the acts were commercial
options.C: The Court held that serious violations of international law remove State immunity
options.D: The Court held that immunity was a rule of procedure and therefore irrelevant to merits

questions.explanation: The Court gave immunity for acts jure imperii, even where grave violations were alleged.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the holding. Option C wrongly labels the acts commercial. Option D confuses the nature of immunity with its irrelevance.
questions.clat_trap: The humane instinct is to deny immunity for atrocities, but the Court did the opposite.
questions.language_trick: 'despite allegations' signals a holding contrary to intuition.

questions.question: A diplomatic agent is sued in a civil action regarding his private flat in the receiving State which he holds for his own use. The agent

options.A: immune unless the sending State waives it impliedly through conduct such as the agent's own participation in the suit
options.B: immune, as diplomats are immune from civil jurisdiction in every action relating to their persons and property in the receiving State
options.C: not immune from civil jurisdiction as to his private immovable property
options.D: immune only if the flat is also used as a part of the embassy or its mission premises for official purposes

questions.explanation: Private immovable property is one of the exceptions to civil immunity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates the immunity. Option B contradicts the rule that waiver must be express. Option D confuses private flat with mission premises.
questions.clat_trap: The words 'impliedly' in one wrong option is aimed at the rule on express waiver.
questions.language_trick: 'impliedly' versus 'expressly' is the language trick in a wrong option.

questions.question: Assertion (A): India, having assured Portugal that Abu Salem would not be sentenced to death or to a term above a set limit, must honour that assurance. Reason (R): The principle of specialty restricts the requesting State to the terms under which the person was extradited.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court tied the assurance to specialty, which binds the requesting State to the terms of surrender.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is the rule from which the obligation in A comes.
questions.clat_trap: A student treats a diplomatic assurance as non-binding on the courts.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following extradition scenarios is LEAST consistent with the principles in the passage?

options.A: A person is extradited on assurances that the death penalty will not be imposed
options.B: A request is declined because the offence is purely political in nature
options.C: A request is declined because the conduct is not an offence in the requested State
options.D: A fraud extraditee is tried for an unrelated political offence

questions.explanation: The first option breaches specialty. The others apply double criminality, the political offence exception and assurances.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies double criminality. Option B applies the political offence exception. Option C reflects a lawful assurance.
questions.clat_trap: The stem says LEAST consistent, so the unlawful scenario is the right answer, though it appears first.
questions.language_trick: 'LEAST consistent' reverses the usual selection logic.

passages.title: Writ Jurisdiction and Public Interest Litigation
passages.passage: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights and is itself a fundamental right. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and for 'any other purpose', thus extending to ordinary legal rights. Writs issued under Article 226 can reach persons and authorities outside the Court's territory if the cause of action arises wholly or in part within it. Habeas corpus tests the legality of detention and may be moved by a third party. Mandamus lies against public authorities to perform a public duty, and a demand and refusal ordinarily precede it; it can be issued to a private body only where it performs a public function. Certiorari corrects jurisdictional errors and errors of law apparent on the face of the record, and prohibition prevents an inferior court from exceeding jurisdiction. Quo warranto lies to challenge the usurpation of a public office of a substantive character created by statute or the Constitution, and any person may move it, since it vindicates a public wrong. Although the existence of an alternative remedy is a factor of self-restraint for the High Court, it is not an absolute bar, and a writ may be entertained where fundamental rights are alleged to be breached, natural justice is violated, the order is wholly without jurisdiction or the vires of a statute is challenged (Whirlpool, 1998). In Daryao (1961), the Supreme Court held that a writ petition decided on its merits by a High Court operates as res judicata for a later petition on the same facts under Article 32, though a dismissal in limine, without a speaking order, does not. Public interest litigation has relaxed the rule of locus standi, allowing a public-spirited person to approach the Court for the benefit of those who cannot, but the Court has cautioned against its misuse for private or political gain and has imposed costs on petitioners who file frivolous petitions.

questions.question: A citizen petitions a High Court to quash the appointment of a person to a statutory office on the ground that he lacks the prescribed qualification. The petitioner has no personal interest in the post. The petition is

options.A: not maintainable, since the petitioner has not shown a personal injury
options.B: not maintainable, since only an unsuccessful candidate may move
options.C: maintainable only if the petitioner first demands the removal from the appointing authority
options.D: maintainable as quo warranto, since any person may challenge usurpation of a public office

questions.explanation: Quo warranto vindicates a public wrong, so locus standi is relaxed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B apply the ordinary personal-injury rule that quo warranto relaxes. Option C imports a mandamus requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The rule that applies to mandamus is applied to quo warranto in the last wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'no personal interest' is meant to test the exception.

questions.question: A High Court dismisses a writ petition in limine, without reasons. The petitioner then approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the same facts. The petition is

options.A: not barred by res judicata, since a summary dismissal does not decide the merits
options.B: barred unless the High Court first grants leave to approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 for the same relief
options.C: barred, because Article 32 cannot be invoked once the remedy under Article 226 has been tried on the same facts
options.D: barred, since a dismissal by a High Court is always final between the parties and binds the Supreme Court as well

questions.explanation: Under Daryao, only a decision on merits operates as res judicata.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the distinction between merits and summary dismissal. Option C makes the remedies mutually exclusive. Option D imports a leave requirement.
questions.clat_trap: 'always' in the first wrong option conceals the distinction between in limine and merits.
questions.language_trick: 'in limine, without reasons' is the key phrase.

questions.question: X, a company running a private school, refuses to admit a child, and a parent seeks mandamus under Article 226. On the passage, the writ

options.A: may issue only if the government holds more than half of its shares
options.B: may issue only if the school performs a public function or duty
options.C: cannot issue against any private body, whatever the nature of the function it performs
options.D: must issue, since education is a fundamental right of the child concerned

questions.explanation: A writ can lie against a private body discharging a public function.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates the exclusion. Option C assumes that the right at stake necessarily makes the school a State authority. Option D invents a shareholding test.
questions.clat_trap: The extreme words 'cannot' and 'must' in the wrong options are the trap.
questions.language_trick: 'only if' creates a test, and the wrong options either deny or assume it.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A High Court may entertain a writ petition despite an available statutory appeal if the order is wholly without jurisdiction. Reason (R): The rule of alternative remedy is a rule of self-restraint and not a bar on the power of the Court.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Whirlpool recognises exceptions, and the rule is one of discretion, which explains why a High Court may still entertain such a petition.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states the nature of the rule, which explains A.
questions.clat_trap: A student treats the alternative remedy as a jurisdictional bar.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A Delhi-based petitioner challenges an order passed by an authority in Mumbai, whose effect is felt only in part in Delhi. The Delhi High Court

options.A: can entertain it because the petitioner is resident in Delhi, whatever the cause of action
options.B: may entertain the petition if a part of the cause of action arises within its territory
options.C: can entertain it only with the consent of the Bombay High Court
options.D: can never entertain it, since the authority is located elsewhere

questions.explanation: Article 226(2) allows a High Court to act if the cause of action arises wholly or in part within its territory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads the territorial limit too strictly. Option C invents a consent requirement. Option D treats residence as sufficient.
questions.clat_trap: A pure residence test is tempting but it is not the constitutional test.
questions.language_trick: 'wholly or in part' is the textual hook.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best statement of the Court's approach to public interest litigation in the passage?

options.A: Standing is relaxed for those who cannot approach the court, but misuse is met with costs
options.B: Any person may seek any relief on any ground, since standing is abolished
options.C: Standing is relaxed, but costs may not be imposed since the petition is in the public interest
options.D: Standing is relaxed only where the State is a respondent and fundamental rights are affected

questions.explanation: The passage links relaxed standing to public benefit and to the power to impose costs.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B overstates the relaxation. Option C adds a condition that is not found in the passage. Option D denies the Court's power of costs.
questions.clat_trap: The third wrong option takes a half-truth (public interest) to a wrong conclusion.
questions.language_trick: 'only where' narrows the rule in an unsupported way.

passages.title: Arbitration: Challenge, Interim Relief and Independence of the Arbitrator
passages.passage: Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a party aggrieved by a domestic award may apply to set it aside under Section 34 on limited grounds, including incapacity, invalid agreement, lack of notice, an award beyond the scope of submission, a composition of the tribunal that is contrary to the agreement, conflict with the public policy of India and, for domestic awards, patent illegality appearing on the face of the award. The application must be made within three months of receipt of the award, extendable by the Court by thirty days on sufficient cause but not beyond. The Court cannot re-appreciate evidence or substitute its view for that of the tribunal. Appeals from orders under Section 34 lie under Section 37 and are narrower still. Under Section 16 the tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, which is the principle of competence-competence. Under Section 9 a party may seek interim measures from a Court before or during arbitral proceedings, but once the tribunal is constituted the Court shall not entertain such an application unless the remedy under Section 17 is inefficacious. Where interim relief is granted before the proceedings begin, arbitration must commence within ninety days. Section 12(5), read with the Seventh Schedule, makes a person ineligible to be an arbitrator if his relationship with a party falls within the Schedule, and the parties may waive this only by an express agreement in writing after the disputes have arisen. In TRF Ltd. (2017) the Supreme Court held that a person who is ineligible cannot nominate another arbitrator, while in Perkins Eastman (2019) it held that a party with an interest in the outcome cannot unilaterally appoint the sole arbitrator. In In re Interplay between Arbitration Agreements and the Stamp Act (2023), a seven-judge Bench held that an unstamped agreement is inadmissible but not void, and that the defect is curable.

questions.question: Party X receives the award on 1 January and files a Section 34 application on 15 May, offering sufficient cause for the delay. The Court

options.A: cannot condone the delay, being outside the three months plus thirty days
options.B: can condone the delay if the other party does not object to the application on the ground of limitation
options.C: can condone the delay up to 90 days from the end of the three-month period within which the application should have been filed
options.D: can condone the delay by any period, since sufficient cause has been shown to the satisfaction of the court

questions.explanation: The three-month period can be extended by thirty days at most. 15 May is beyond about 4 months.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the cap. Option C uses the figure from Section 9 for a different purpose. Option D makes the rule depend on consent.
questions.clat_trap: The use of 'sufficient cause' tempts the student to apply the Limitation Act's liberal approach.
questions.language_trick: 'but not beyond' in the passage fixes the outer limit.

questions.question: Which of the following, if found by the Court in a Section 34 application against a domestic award, is a permissible ground?

options.A: An erroneous appreciation of evidence by the tribunal
options.B: Patent illegality appearing on the face of the award
options.C: A finding on facts unsupported by the weight of evidence
options.D: A view of the contract different from the tribunal's though plausible

questions.explanation: Only patent illegality is within Section 34(2A). Re-appreciation of evidence is barred.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D describe merits review, which is excluded.
questions.clat_trap: All the wrong options sound like 'illegality' to a student who treats Section 34 as an appeal.
questions.language_trick: 'patent' and 'on the face' make the illegality visible without reappreciating evidence.

questions.question: An arbitration clause allows the managing director of a company to appoint the sole arbitrator. A dispute arises. The better view under the passage is that

options.A: the appointment is void, and the whole arbitration agreement fails
options.B: the appointment is valid, as the parties agreed to it in the contract
options.C: the appointment is vulnerable, as a party with an interest in the outcome cannot unilaterally appoint the sole arbitrator
options.D: the appointment is valid unless the other party shows actual bias

questions.explanation: Perkins Eastman and TRF bar an interested person from appointing. The agreement to arbitrate survives, and the court may appoint.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores independence. Option B demands proof of actual bias. Option D says the whole agreement fails.
questions.clat_trap: Party autonomy is a strong instinct, but it yields to impartiality. The last wrong option overstates the consequence.
questions.language_trick: 'vulnerable' is a careful word, 'void' is not.

questions.question: A tribunal has been constituted and a party applies to a Court under Section 9 for an interim injunction. The Court should

options.A: grant it, since the tribunal cannot enforce its own orders in any case
options.B: refuse it, since the Court has no power at all after the tribunal is constituted
options.C: decline the application, unless it is shown that the remedy before the tribunal is inefficacious
options.D: grant it, since Section 9 is available at any stage

questions.explanation: After constitution, the Court shall not entertain the application unless Section 17 is inefficacious.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the limit after constitution. Option B overstates the weakness of Section 17. Option D ignores the inefficacy exception.
questions.clat_trap: 'at any stage' and 'no power at all' are both extreme options on either side of the correct middle.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A party that wishes to rely on a Seventh Schedule relationship to disqualify an arbitrator can be held to have waived it by conduct during the proceedings. Reason (R): Section 12(5) permits waiver only by an express agreement in writing made after disputes have arisen.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Waiver by conduct is not permitted. A is false. R states the statutory rule.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a correct statement of the proviso, and it is what makes A false.
questions.clat_trap: A student applies the general principle of waiver by participation.
questions.language_trick: 'by conduct' and 'express agreement in writing' are mutually exclusive.

questions.question: A party objects that the arbitration agreement is invalid. The first forum to decide the objection under the scheme of the passage is

options.A: a civil court, which must stay the arbitration meanwhile
options.B: the arbitral tribunal under Section 16, subject to later challenge under Section 34
options.C: the Supreme Court under Section 37, since it relates to a jurisdictional question
options.D: the High Court under Section 9, as the validity of the agreement is a legal question

questions.explanation: Competence-competence allows the tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction first.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A misplaces Section 9, which relates to interim measures. Option C misplaces Section 37, which is an appellate provision. Option D stops the arbitration without authority.
questions.clat_trap: The sections cited in the wrong options are real, but they perform different functions.
questions.language_trick: 'first forum' is the order of decision, not the final one.

passages.title: Hazardous Industry, Absolute Liability and the National Green Tribunal
passages.passage: The Bhopal gas leak of December 1984 led to the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985, under which the Union acted as parens patriae for victims, and to a settlement of USD 470 million in 1989 approved by the Supreme Court. In 2023 a Constitution Bench dismissed the Union's curative petition seeking additional compensation from the successors of the company, holding that a settlement cannot be reopened without a ground of fraud or similar vitiating factor. After the Oleum gas leak in Delhi, the Court in M.C. Mehta (1987) held that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is absolutely liable to compensate those harmed, without the exceptions recognised in Rylands v. Fletcher, and that the compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise. The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 imposes no-fault liability on the owner of a hazardous substance to pay relief for death or injury and requires insurance. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 established the National Green Tribunal (NGT) with jurisdiction over civil cases involving a substantial question relating to the environment which arise under the seven laws listed in Schedule I, which include the Water Act, the Air Act, the Environment Protection Act, the Forest (Conservation) Act and the Public Liability Insurance Act, but exclude the Wildlife Protection Act and the Indian Forest Act, 1927. The NGT is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or the Evidence Act, and follows natural justice and the principles of sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays. An appeal from its orders lies to the Supreme Court within ninety days. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996) the Court held that precaution and polluter pays form part of the law of the land under Articles 21, 47, 48A and 51A(g). In Ankita Sinha (2021) the Supreme Court held that the NGT may exercise suo motu powers, as the Act is meant to secure effective disposal of environmental disputes.

questions.question: A factory handling a toxic gas suffers a leak caused by sabotage by an unknown stranger, and neighbours are harmed. Under M.C. Mehta's rule of absolute liability, the enterprise

options.A: is liable only to the extent of its insurance cover, which fixes the ceiling of compensation
options.B: is liable, as absolute liability admits no stranger exception
options.C: is liable only if the victims prove that it was negligent in the guarding of the gas
options.D: is not liable, since the act of a stranger breaks the chain of causation between enterprise and harm

questions.explanation: Absolute liability has no exceptions of the Rylands type.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the Rylands exception. Option C adds negligence. Option D treats insurance as the cap.
questions.clat_trap: A student applies Rylands-type exceptions to a rule that was designed to exclude them.
questions.language_trick: 'sabotage by an unknown stranger' is a deliberate pointer to an excluded defence.

questions.question: Which dispute falls within the NGT's jurisdiction as set out in the passage?

options.A: A complaint of noise nuisance under a municipal bye-law raising a private dispute
options.B: A claim for compensation for the felling of trees under the Indian Forest Act, 1927, pursued by a forest department
options.C: A prosecution for poaching under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, brought against several members of an organised hunting gang
options.D: A civil case on effluent discharge into a river under the Water Act, raising a substantial environmental question

questions.explanation: The Water Act is in Schedule I, whereas the Wildlife Protection Act and the 1927 Forest Act are excluded.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B involve excluded laws. Option C lacks a scheduled statute and a substantial question.
questions.clat_trap: Wildlife and forest laws are intuitively 'environmental', but the Schedule excludes them.
questions.language_trick: 'Indian Forest Act, 1927' vs 'Forest (Conservation) Act' is the trap.

questions.question: On the Bhopal curative petition (2023), the passage's position is that

options.A: the Court held that the settlement was void, since the Union lacked the power to represent the victims before the Court
options.B: the Court dismissed the Union's plea, since a settlement may not be reopened without fraud or a like vitiating factor
options.C: the Court allowed additional compensation, on the ground that the 1989 estimate of the number of victims was too low
options.D: the Court directed the successors of the company to pay, since absolute liability continues indefinitely against them

questions.explanation: The Court refused to reopen the settlement for want of fraud.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option D reverse the result. Option C invents a holding on the Union's power.
questions.clat_trap: A student's sympathy for the victims pushes towards the reversed outcome.
questions.language_trick: 'dismissed the Union's plea' is the first thing to read.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Under the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, a victim of an accident involving a hazardous substance need not prove negligence of the owner to claim relief. Reason (R): The Act imposes no-fault liability on the owner of the hazardous substance.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: No-fault liability dispenses with proof of fault, which explains why negligence need not be proved.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is the statutory basis for A.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'insurance' leads a student to think the victim must prove a claim against an insurer.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The NGT, on reading a newspaper report of an illegal sand-mining operation damaging a river, begins proceedings on its own motion. Under the passage, the NGT's action is

options.A: beyond its powers, as the Tribunal may act only on an application made by an aggrieved person or authority
options.B: within its powers only if the Supreme Court has first issued directions on the subject to the State concerned
options.C: within its powers, as Ankita Sinha recognised suo motu power for effective disposal of disputes
options.D: within its powers only if the Central Government refers the matter to it by a notification under the statute

questions.explanation: Ankita Sinha held that the NGT may exercise suo motu power.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reflects the older view the Court rejected. Option B and Option D add conditions that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The statute does not state suo motu powers in terms, so the first wrong option is tempting.
questions.language_trick: 'recognised' signals a judicial reading and not an express provision.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an accurate statement about the NGT on the passage?

options.A: It is bound strictly by the Code of Civil Procedure
